evidence_sentence: for our ACL 2021 camera-ready manuscript, as Ramesh and I began our checks yesterday.
full_email_context: Thread ID: 7RGC9D Mail ID: MAIL56RZ3N2L Date: 3rd September 2021 From: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> Subject: Formatting & Cross-Referencing Update for ACL 2021 Submission  Dear all,  I wanted to provide a quick update on the progress of the formatting and section cross-referencing review for our ACL 2021 camera-ready manuscript, as Ramesh and I began our checks yesterday. We have completed a preliminary pass through the main document and appendices, focusing on the following areas:  1. **Template Adherence:** The latest ACL 2021 template guidelines are now fully integrated into the Overleaf project. All section headers, figure placements, and reference formatting have been standardized. I have flagged a few instances where margin notes exceeded word count limits, and made preliminary trims in the compliance appendix footnotes.  2. **Cross-Referencing:** All intra-textual references (e.g., cross-links between Section 4 and the compliance appendix, and citations to illustrative case studies) have been tested and are resolving correctly in the current build. One minor issue remains with dynamic numbering of supplementary materials—Michael, could you double-check the auto-generated labels in the compliance checklist subsection?  3. **Section Numbering/Consistency Issues:** Ramesh and I found two small inconsistencies in the section numbering, likely due to the Overleaf macro updates. I have corrected these, but please notify us if any manual overrides have been introduced subsequently.  4. **DOI and Repository Links:** Sunita, thank you for providing the updated list of dataset DOIs and repository links. I have cross-checked these in-text and in the references, but kindly reconfirm their accessibility before final integration. Michael, if the embargo statement includes any new resource URLs, please insert them in the shared reference file.  We are on schedule according to our internal timeline. Please continue to log any minor corrections (stylistic, typographical, etc.) directly in Overleaf by 5 February; after this, we intend to lock the sections for final harmonization and camera-ready migration.  If any of you spot outstanding compliance or template issues, or if further clarification is required on specific formatting points, do not hesitate to reach out on email or Slack.  Best regards,  Ananya Chatterjee   Department of Computer Science   University of Oxford

full_email_context: Thread ID: 5X6UXH Mail ID: MAIL03VUWEN4 Date: 14th November 2024 From: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> Subject: Re: Pre-Meeting: Methodology Update and Outstanding Queries  Dear Sunita, Michael, and Ramesh,  Thank you, Sunita, for your comprehensive progress update and for raising timely queries before our scheduled meeting tomorrow. I appreciate everyone’s ongoing attention to detail, which will be crucial as we consolidate our responses for the major revision.  Let me address your questions point by point:  1. **Space Restrictions:** Based on my review of recent JOCCH issues, the editorial office exhibits flexibility for the inclusion of extended methodological appendices, especially when such detail supports reproducibility and transparency in data-centric submissions. For the main text, we need to remain within the usual 10,000-word limit, but supplementary materials (uploaded as appendices) can host corpus tables, extended annotation rationales, and additional reliability metrics. I suggest highlighting key findings and summary statistics in the body, while relegating exhaustive details and raw data breakdowns to the appendix. This not only adheres to JOCCH’s requirements but should also satisfy the reviewers’ requests without overloading the main narrative.  2. **Visualization Consistency:** Michael, unless you have identified any interpretability issues with our previous color schema, my recommendation is to maintain consistency for cross-comparability. If you do make significant updates for improved clarity (particularly for temporal analyses), please ensure that the color legend is intuitive and clearly documented in all figure captions and supplementary explanations. I am happy to review draft visualizations before they are finalized for layout uniformity.  3. **Legal Clauses:** Ramesh’s compilation of recent amendments for India’s Data Protection Bill will be invaluable. Ramesh, could you flag the latest updates regarding archival data annotation—especially references to researcher obligations for cross-regional data and subject consent? Sunita, once Ramesh shares the relevant clauses, please integrate direct citations and—if space allows—a summary in a compliance footnote within the methods section, with further context in the supplementary material as needed.  Sunita, sharing a working draft and corpus tables by Monday evening will be perfect; this will give all of us a chance to review and prepare for a targeted discussion during the meeting. If feasible, please upload preliminary appendix content as clearly labeled drafts in the drive.  Thank you all again for your commitment to this revision. Let’s aim to confirm our section updates and finalize the rebuttal outline in tomorrow’s call, keeping momentum toward our 30 November deadline.  Best, Ananya  Dr. Ananya Chatterjee   Department of Computer Science   University of Oxford

full_email_context: Thread ID: BQ99XT Mail ID: MAILDYQ4G2M7 Date: 27th March 2025 From: Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> Subject: Next Steps: Outlining for Methods Note/Short-Form Submission  Dear Sunita, Ananya, and Michael,  Thank you, Sunita, for confirming the colloquium abstract submission and for sharing both the finalized document and memo; these will serve as valuable reference points for our next phase. I want to take this opportunity to reiterate my appreciation for your rigorous input and collaborative engagement throughout the memo preparation and departmental submission processes.  As we await feedback from the colloquium committee, I suggest we begin concretely outlining the proposed methods note or short-form paper, given our consensus on its relevance and potential impact. Building on Ananya’s and Michael’s earlier messages, I propose the following provisional steps:  1. **Identify Core Contributions**: Focusing the manuscript around our multi-author version management schema and reviewer feedback cycle—areas in which our workflow diverges from standard NLP practice on historical corpora—should make for a compelling technical communication or system demonstration.  2. **Venue Selection**: Since we are weighing both EMNLP System Demonstrations and JDoc Technical Communication, I recommend we draft a two-paragraph rationale/motivation for each, including the target audience, and evaluate which best matches our methodological innovations and the desired scope of impact.  3. **Detailed Outline**: I would like each co-author to add bullet points in a shared document (new Google Doc to be created) by 8 April addressing:    - Unique challenges and solutions in multi-institutional NLP workflow documentation,    - A stepwise breakdown of our version management/reviewer handling process,    - Supplementary material (e.g., workflow diagrams, sample log excerpts, cross-institutional compliance best practices).  4. **Meeting Suggestion**: If agreeable, we could schedule a brief Zoom meeting post-8 April to finalize the outline and make a decision on the submission venue based on our collective evaluation.  Please let me know your availability for a virtual meeting (suggested dates: 10 or 11 April) and any preferences or proposed additions to the outline components above. Once consensus on the outline is reached, we can delegate writing tasks in the same collaborative spirit as our previous memo effort.  Looking forward to your thoughts and to further impactful collaboration.  Best regards,  Ramesh  Prof. Ramesh Bhatia   Department of Computer Science   Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

full_email_context: Thread ID: 98OB6N Mail ID: MAILU9F7S6PM Date: 21st April 2022 From: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in> To: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> Subject: IACS Review and Additions to Scenario Supplement – Press Query Protocol & Consortium Adoption  Dear Ananya, Michael, and Prof. Bhatia,  Thank you both for your detailed and valuable annotations, and for spearheading the integration of proactive case scenarios into our evolving press query response resource. I have thoroughly reviewed the latest “Working_Draft_Scenarios” in the shared folder and appreciate the inclusion of both Stanford’s and Oxford’s compliance perspectives.  From the IACS standpoint, I suggest we supplement the section on early access requests with a note regarding India’s “Right to Information” (RTI) provisions as they occasionally generate external outreach in research collaborations, especially for data sourced from national archives. I have articulated a draft response pathway under the “Media Queries Originating Under RTI” heading, which details referral processes to IACS legal counsel and recommends embargo log reference to substantiate temporary access restrictions.  Additionally, for scenarios involving regional press escalation—particularly during major conferences like JCDL 2022—I recommend a protocol for rapid English-to-Hindi translation of key compliance messages. This may be appended as an advisory within the supplement, ensuring our communication remains accessible and responsive to local contexts.  Regarding your question, Ananya, my preference would be to append this scenario supplement as a formal annex to the finalized press query response template, especially since our communications teams often prefer a single consolidated reference file. However, I defer to Prof. Bhatia’s judgement for final formatting and distribution.  If everyone agrees, I am happy to compile the consolidated annex and circulate a unified draft by 29 October for final team review and sign-off.  Looking forward to your approval or further recommendations.  Best regards,  Sunita  Sunita Sen   PhD Scholar   Department of Computer Science   Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

Special thanks to Sunita for taking the initiative to circulate a preliminary outline for our workshop report. After reviewing all the analytics, feedback, and resource materials uploaded to “Workshop2022_Analytics,” I am writing to propose the next steps for collaboratively developing our manuscript for potential submission to JCDL or JOCCH.  Here is a suggested refinement of Sunita’s outline, incorporating our collective feedback and the detailed points discussed yesterday:  1. **Introduction & Motivation** – Framing the historical NLP challenges and aims of the workshop (Lead: Ananya) 2. **Workshop Design & Accessibility Protocols** – Detailed documentation of our inclusive design, participant support pathways, and results from real-time accessibility interventions (Lead: Sunita, supported by Michael) 3. **Dataset Overview** – Description of the historical corpora provided, mirroring infrastructure, and lessons from cross-regional access (Lead: Michael) 4. **Q&A Moderation & Technical Escalation Framework** – Analysis of live Q&A workflows, escalation scenarios, chat analytics, and moderator guidelines (Lead: Ramesh, supported by Sunita) 5. **Participant Feedback Analysis & Outcomes** – Synthesis of pre- and post-event surveys, chat transcripts, and satisfaction metrics (Lead: Ananya and Sunita) 6. **Lessons Learned & Recommendations** – Cross-cutting insights, future improvements, and formal citation protocols (co-drafted; lead to be decided) 7. **Appendices** – Example survey instruments, accessibility guidelines, and moderator scripts.  We agreed on a first draft target deadline of 4th November 2020. Please let me know if you are comfortable with your suggested sections or would like to adjust responsibilities. Once confirmed, I will create dedicated folders for each section in our shared drive and propose a brief check-in call around 10 June to synchronize progress and discuss emerging questions.  Finally, as discussed, let’s keep open the possibility of dual submission—either as workshop proceedings (JCDL 2022) or to JOCCH as a full-length reflective article, depending on group consensus. We can review their respective deadlines at our next meeting.  Thank you again for your remarkable teamwork. I look forward to working closely with all of you over the coming fortnight as we transform our workshop experience into a valuable scholarly contribution.  Best regards,  Ramesh  Prof. Ramesh Bhatia   Department of Computer Science   Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

full_email_context: Thread ID: PT6P9L Mail ID: MAIL3R8KYPD2 Date: 13th January 2024 From: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in> To: Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> Subject: Reflection Memo Meeting Minutes & Next Steps  Dear all,  Thank you for a productive meeting earlier today and for all your diligent preparations leading into our discussion. I’m writing to summarize the key action points and decisions (please correct or supplement as needed):  1. **Section Leads Confirmed:**    - Michael: Overview/introduction and US-side compliance practices    - Ananya: UK data negotiation and international harmonization    - Ramesh: Institutional ethical approval documentation and comparative analysis    - Sunita (myself): Details of the NDLI access workflow, annual data licensing, and drafting recommendations on multi-year data sharing agreements  2. **Appendices:**    - Ramesh will upload the anonymized IACS ethics committee correspondences.    - Ananya and Michael will collate UK and Stanford sample artifacts, respectively, for appendix inclusion.  3. **Drafting Timeline:**    - Everyone to populate their assigned outline sections by 14 November.    - Review of draft material and asynchronous comments from 15–18 November.    - Circulate consolidated draft by 20 November for final team review.  4. **Data-sharing Discussion:**    - We agreed the memo should devote a specific subsection to evolving practices in multi-year data and compliance arrangements, noting the newly introduced annual review processes with the West Bengal State Archives and Stanford IRB.  5. **Grant Application Alignment:**    - Michael raised the useful point of explicitly aligning this memo’s recommendations with the anticipated DST and UKRI reporting templates.  6. **Next Meeting:**     - Tentatively scheduled for 21 November (same time slot), pending confirmation of everyone’s schedule and progress on the draft.  Please let me know if I missed any details or if corrections are needed. I will take the lead on compiling these notes and updating our shared Google Doc with the agreed-upon version.  Once again, thank you all for your collegiality and rigorous collaboration on this internal reflection memo. Looking forward to your contributions to the draft and to continued positive momentum on both our publication and future projects.  Best regards,  Sunita  Sunita Sen   PhD Scholar   Department of Computer Science   Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

full_email_context: Thread ID: ONU3NA Mail ID: MAIL44GJP7SA Date: 28th November 2022 From: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> Subject: Coordination Call Confirmation & Further Reviewer Preparation  Dear Sunita, Ramesh, and Michael,  Thank you, Sunita, for your outstanding work in compiling the initial reviewer response points and for taking the initiative to structure our draft document in the shared drive. I have just reviewed your uploaded “JOCCH2022_Reviewer_Response_Preparation” document, and your detailed explanations provide an excellent foundation for our coordinated responses.  Regarding the proposed coordination call, Thursday at 16:00 IST (09:30 BST, 01:30 PDT) works for me. A brief meeting at that time should give us an opportunity to discuss any final concerns, distribute action items, and ensure that our draft bullet points address reviewer expectations comprehensively. Please, Michael and Ramesh, confirm your availability for this slot.  In preparation for the call, I suggest we each review and, where relevant, refine or elaborate on specific sections of the response draft. In particular, we should aim to: - Cross-link the dataset description points to our supplementary table references for ease of reviewer verification, - Strengthen the discussion on annotation reliability by including artifact examples (with sensitive information redacted), - Prepare a brief outline of how evaluation metrics generalize to novel dialectal input (perhaps referencing our codebase modularity or pipeline diagrams).  Sunita, please go ahead and send around the Google Meet invitation once we have everyone’s confirmation. If anyone thinks additional agenda items should be included for the call, let me know by Wednesday evening.  Thank you all for your collaboration as we move toward the peer review stage.  Best regards,  Ananya  Dr. Ananya Chatterjee   Department of Computer Science   University of Oxford

evidence_sentence: in advance of the final draft assembly for JOCCH.
full_email_context: Thread ID: 0YQMMP Mail ID: MAILF123TJQM Date: 21st June 2024 From: Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> Subject: Coordination Call Summary & Next Steps Towards JOCCH Submission  Dear Sunita, Ananya, and Ramesh,  Thank you for your participation in yesterday’s coordination call and for the excellent preparation that has brought us to fruition on nearly every checklist item. I am sending this summary both for documentation and as a final confirmation of our roles and next actions in advance of the final draft assembly for JOCCH.  **Key Outcomes from 11 May Call:** 1. **Final Checklist Sign-Off:** All participants confirmed approval on the checklist, with a minor clarification on the embargo status of one dataset subset—which Sunita will address (with Ramesh) in the compliance appendix before sign-off by 18 May. 2. **Manuscript Assembly:** Ananya will coordinate collation of the stable manuscript sections and circulate the compiled draft by 28 May. Michael (myself) will provide a final review of Zenodo metadata and supplementary legal documentation. 3. **Cover Letter Drafting:** Sunita has volunteered to circulate a cover letter template with emphasis on legal compliance and the meta-annotation methodology, taking into account recent JOCCH recommendations. Target: first draft circulation by 17 May. 4. **Author Order and Contributions:** Consensus reached—author order accurately reflects labor distribution and all corresponding author metadata is updated. 5. **Zenodo Project Status:** Final embargo confirmation and typo checks are complete (Sunita/Michael). Zenodo link and citation format to be embedded in both the manuscript and cover letter.  **Immediate Next Steps:** - Sunita to confirm and document embargo status in the compliance appendix and initiate cover letter drafting. - Ananya to integrate all finalized contributions and address any outstanding author notes. - All to review the compiled submission package (including cover letter) by 28 May and provide any last feedback.  I am optimistic that, with this momentum, we will submit a robust and exemplary resource note ahead of the JOCCH cycle. Please let me or Ananya know if you anticipate any issues on timing or require access to updated institutional templates.  Thank you again for your trust, diligence, and truly collegial collaboration. Looking forward to a strong final push.  Best regards,  Michael  Dr. Michael Bradley   Department of Computer Science   Stanford University

full_email_context: Thread ID: 72R3K7 Mail ID: MAILR5V1QSN9 Date: 29th October 2020 From: Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> Subject: Feedback on Domain Shift Analysis Draft and Anchor Schematic  Dear Sunita, Ramesh, and Ananya,  Thank you, Sunita, for circulating the drafts for both the domain shift analysis and the code anchor schematic. I have carefully reviewed “DomainTransfer_Limits_v1_Feb2021.docx” and the accompanying figures. The quantitative expansion is thorough and provides clear insight into the limits of model transfer—especially the statistical confidence intervals and the contextualization of performance drops during cross-lingual application.  I have added in-line suggestions for clarifying some of the statistical terminology and propose specifying the minimum support threshold per label in your plotted outlier cases for transparency. The supplementary commentary you included on calibration drift is strong; I recommend integrating a short paragraph that contrasts these findings against previous literature benchmarks (see comments referencing Domingos et al., 2019) to further satisfy Reviewer 1’s call for explicit transferability limits. The plots in Figures 3a–3c are well constructed. Adjusting the y-axis annotation to underscore the critical points where transferability degrades (e.g., below F1=0.6) may make the narrative more compelling.  Regarding the code anchor schematic: the visual is clear, and I agree with Ananya that the logical mapping between anchor indices and methods subsections is intuitive. You might consider highlighting (perhaps with color-coding) how reviewer cues directly correspond to the manuscript sub-sections and code cells—this would address the reviewer’s request for navigational clarity.  Ramesh, the upcoming compliance and anonymization updates will complement these additions well. Please let me know if you’d like a technical read-through of your draft once it’s ready.  Overall, I am optimistic that these revisions will fully deliver on the requested clarifications. Let’s plan to integrate our latest updates by 8 February to ensure sufficient time for pre-submission review ahead of the deadline.  Kind regards,  Michael

full_email_context: Thread ID: 72R3K7 Mail ID: MAILR5V1QSN9 Date: 29th October 2020 From: Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> Subject: Feedback on Domain Shift Analysis Draft and Anchor Schematic  Dear Sunita, Ramesh, and Ananya,  Thank you, Sunita, for circulating the drafts for both the domain shift analysis and the code anchor schematic. I have carefully reviewed “DomainTransfer_Limits_v1_Feb2021.docx” and the accompanying figures. The quantitative expansion is thorough and provides clear insight into the limits of model transfer—especially the statistical confidence intervals and the contextualization of performance drops during cross-lingual application.  I have added in-line suggestions for clarifying some of the statistical terminology and propose specifying the minimum support threshold per label in your plotted outlier cases for transparency. The supplementary commentary you included on calibration drift is strong; I recommend integrating a short paragraph that contrasts these findings against previous literature benchmarks (see comments referencing Domingos et al., 2019) to further satisfy Reviewer 1’s call for explicit transferability limits. The plots in Figures 3a–3c are well constructed. Adjusting the y-axis annotation to underscore the critical points where transferability degrades (e.g., below F1=0.6) may make the narrative more compelling.  Regarding the code anchor schematic: the visual is clear, and I agree with Ananya that the logical mapping between anchor indices and methods subsections is intuitive. You might consider highlighting (perhaps with color-coding) how reviewer cues directly correspond to the manuscript sub-sections and code cells—this would address the reviewer’s request for navigational clarity.  Ramesh, the upcoming compliance and anonymization updates will complement these additions well. Please let me know if you’d like a technical read-through of your draft once it’s ready.  Overall, I am optimistic that these revisions will fully deliver on the requested clarifications. Let’s plan to integrate our latest updates by 8 February to ensure sufficient time for pre-submission review ahead of the deadline.  Kind regards,  Michael

full_email_context: Thread ID: BZRV4O Mail ID: MAILX4C2JKL5 Date: 29th September 2024 From: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in> To: Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> Subject: Technical Note Planning & Next Steps  Dear Michael, Ramesh, and Ananya,  Thank you for your encouraging feedback and concrete proposals regarding post-submission outreach and the technical note. I am enthused by the idea of documenting our compliance workflow and rolling embargo best practices in a focused preprint or repository note. Michael, I appreciate your offer to coordinate outreach and possible institutional press engagements—this should amplify both our visibility and the practical utility of our approach for other historical NLP projects.  Regarding the technical note: - I propose we scope the document as a short, how-to guide—supplemented by annotated examples taken from our JOCCH revision, e.g., citation blocks, sample Zenodo accession calls, and walkthroughs of the embargo timeline schematic. We could also include recommendations on collaborating with institutional legal teams for sustainable data release. - I am happy to take a first pass at outlining the core content by 15 September, drawing on materials from our shared drive and referencing reviewer suggestions we received during the JOCCH process. It would be helpful if each of you could suggest specific points or illustrative figures you’d like included. - Michael, I can draft an annotated slide outline jointly with you and circulate it for input, so it dovetails well with a prospective virtual seminar. Ananya and Ramesh, your perspectives on legal and policy communication would be invaluable for the guidance sections.  For outreach, I have also started compiling contact details for pertinent ACM SIGs, digital humanities newsletters, and heritage curation forums. Once our JOCCH article is formally accepted, we should coordinate a press release, as well as a blog post or news update for the IACS and Stanford websites.  Finally, as soon as we have a response from the JOCCH editorial office, I suggest we schedule a group call to finalize authorship and distribution for the preprint, and review the virtual seminar format options for October. Please share your availability for a potential call during the third week of September.  Looking forward to your thoughts and continued collaboration.  Best regards,  Sunita  Sunita Sen   PhD Scholar   Department of Computer Science   Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

object_label: prepare extended version of ACL2024 paper
evidence_sentence: I strongly support the idea of preparing an extended version
full_email_context: Thread ID: SXWNW8 Mail ID: MAILAG52RJKT Date: 22nd May 2024 From: Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> Subject: Planning Meeting for Journal Extension & Outreach Strategy  Dear Sunita, Ramesh, and Ananya,  Thank you, Sunita, for your thoughtful message and for initiating the conversation regarding our post-ACL trajectory. Congratulations once again to all on reaching this significant milestone with our ACL2024 paper!  I strongly support the idea of preparing an extended version, and both JOCCH and Journal of Documentation would be excellent targets given their strong focus on digital scholarship, archival methodologies, and the intersection of NLP with cultural heritage. I am particularly keen on including the analyses you mentioned—especially the sub-dialectal code-switching patterns and the longitudinal adaptation studies, which were well received during internal reviews but couldn’t fit within the ACL page constraints. We could also consider elaborating on our annotation guidelines and historic language normalization pipeline, as these could benefit subsequent researchers in the field.  On outreach, a formal resource paper to accompany the dataset release is timely—perhaps even a separate dataset note or technical report that could be cross-referenced in our main paper. We should strategize how to maximize visibility and community reusability (maybe via Zenodo and the LDC catalog) and outline a modest user study to track uptake.  Regarding a planning meeting, the week of 22 April works well for me. Specifically, I propose we convene on Thursday, 24 April, at 16:00 GMT. I can send a Zoom invitation as soon as the date is confirmed by everyone. The agenda could include: - Journal extension structure & division of new writing tasks - Dataset/resource paper logistics and timeline - Outreach to the broader historical NLP community - Preliminary organization of our upcoming ACL2024 presentation  Please confirm whether 24 April, 16:00 GMT, is convenient, or suggest alternatives. In the meantime, I’ll begin drafting a brief outline for the extended version and collate feedback on dataset dissemination channels.  Looking forward to our continued collaboration!  Best, Michael  Dr. Michael Bradley   Department of Computer Science   Stanford University

full_email_context: Thread ID: G3612I Mail ID: MAILK3D9PZI7 Date: 10th May 2019 From: Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> To: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> CC: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> Subject: Visualization Inputs and Accessibility Notes  Dear Ananya,  Thank you for initiating the process for our draft visualizations and for your dedication to accessibility and privacy compliance. I support Sunita’s recommendation to use anonymized participant IDs in all figures and legends, which aligns well with best practices and the requirements of both ACL and EMNLP submissions.  Regarding your question on color accessibility: I would indeed endorse the use of a colorblind-friendly palette such as “viridis” or “plasma” (both available in matplotlib). These palettes not only improve interpretability for reviewers with color vision deficiencies but also generally yield figures with cleaner contrasts for publication. Our institute currently does not mandate a specific color scheme for collaborative outputs, so please proceed with your judgment, prioritizing clarity and inclusivity.  For key examples: Sunita’s suggestions are excellent, and I would only add that, for the “edge case” from Document F, it would be beneficial to visually annotate the section where the faithfulness rating notably dropped (perhaps by using a contrasting outline or marker), explicitly linking it with the corresponding margin note from Dr. Patel. This could help reviewers quickly grasp the impact of document noise on our model’s interpretability metrics.  Lastly, if possible, please ensure that all figure captions explicitly explain the color scales and any highlighting conventions used, as this will further facilitate reviewer understanding.  We look forward to reviewing your draft figures. Thank you for your continued leadership on this critical aspect of our human evaluation section.  Best regards,   Ramesh

I am pleased to submit the following summary points from IACS for potential inclusion in the bulletin:  1. **Societal Relevance and Outreach**: “Our NLP-based framework bridges the academic and public history divide, enabling digitized archives in regional languages to be more broadly searchable and accessible. This accelerates grassroots historical research and aids community-driven archival initiatives across South Asia.” 2. **Research Vision**: “By combining domain-specific language modeling with scalable digitization pipelines, our project lays vital groundwork not only for academic historians but also for educators, librarians, and policy-makers concerned with heritage preservation.” 3. **Next Steps**: “Looking forward, IACS remains committed to fostering partnerships for technical knowledge transfer, especially toward building multilingual tools for less-resourced cultural datasets.”  Please review and let me know if any phrasing should be adjusted for alignment with the overall bulletin tone. If you wish to combine or reformat these statements for brevity, feel free to do so. Sunita, I copied you in case the communications office needs any additional background information or quick follow-up.  Michael, I will update the media monitoring sheet with the latest local coverage links, as we had a story in The Telegraph (India) that deserves mention. Ananya, thank you for your editorial leadership on this; I look forward to seeing the finalized material before submission.  With best regards,  Ramesh Bhatia   Professor and Project PI   Department of Computer Science   Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

I suggest using a colorblind-friendly scheme, but will be happy to adapt to house style if needed. 3. Finally, are there any exemplar explanatory segments—especially those flagged as “highly actionable” or “uncertain due to noise”—that the team feels strongly about highlighting in the vignette figure? Please send your recommendations by the 17th so they can be incorporated.  Once I have feedback on these points, I will proceed with draft visualizations and upload them to our shared Drive for comments. Please feel free to reach out if there are any additional specifics you would like addressed regarding figure format or alignment with target conference guidelines.  Looking forward to collaborating on this critical section of our submission.  Best regards, Ananya

full_email_context: Thread ID: WOGRJV Mail ID: MAILE8J45LMC Date: 9th June 2024 From: Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> To: Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu>, Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> Subject: Student-Led Project Legal Notice Template & Documentation Progress  Dear Michael, Sunita, and Ananya,  I am pleased to confirm that the draft of the “Student-Led Project Legal Notice” has been completed ahead of schedule and is now available in the shared folder (“2024_JournalExtension/LegalNotices/”). The template adheres to Zenodo’s guidelines for dataset submissions and includes explicit language on (i) consortium authorship, (ii) international usage and licensing caveats, and (iii) privacy and data minimization practices. The notice is designed for both inclusion in our resource manuscript appendix and upload as a supplementary PDF to the primary Zenodo record.  Michael, thank you for advancing the Zenodo project page and for your attention to draft metadata. I have reviewed the initial entry and—apart from the formatted legal notice upload—foresee no substantive obstacles given our current institutional authorizations. I recommend we finalize the point-of-contact emails and institutional affiliations for all contributors; please ensure Ananya’s preferred Oxford affiliation is reflected, and do highlight any co-authoring conventions required by JOCCH for dataset notes.  Sunita, I want to acknowledge your prompt feedback on cross-validation. The latest meta-annotation review (version “MetaAnnoLog_v5May.docx”) is now integrated with minor clarifying comments—if you or Michael identify additional edge cases prior to the 5 May deadline, we can append an addendum for transparency.  Ananya, your ongoing editorial oversight is much appreciated. As soon as you add final clarifying footnotes to the normalization section, please notify the group so we can flag that portion as stable for manuscript compilation.  Barring any urgent queries or additional partner requests before our 2 June draft milestone, we are well positioned for a complete and compliant JOCCH submission. Please let me know if anyone anticipates travel or leave that might require timeline adjustments within the next fortnight.  With thanks for everyone’s diligence and coordination,  Best regards,  Ramesh  Prof. Ramesh Bhatia   Department of Computer Science   Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

evidence_sentence: Thank you, Sunita and Michael, for your thorough and thoughtful approaches to post-submission outreach and collaborative plans.
full_email_context: Thread ID: 8GYOIA Mail ID: MAILEM9JG842 Date: 24th September 2022 From: Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> Subject: Re: Post-Submission Plan & Coordination on Dissemination Activities  Dear Sunita, Michael, and Ananya,  Thank you, Sunita and Michael, for your thorough and thoughtful approaches to post-submission outreach and collaborative plans. I completely agree that now is the right time to prepare our dissemination and follow-up strategies while we await the JCDL decision.  On dissemination, Sunita’s observations on compliance are spot-on. Sharing a high-level summary or analysis—carefully avoiding embargoed material—would benefit both our professional networks and the wider digital humanities community. Michael, your offer to draft a blog-style summary is much appreciated. I am happy to review/edit, particularly with regard to correctly communicating our methodology and ensuring that the intended audience (which may include non-technical readers) is effectively engaged.  Regarding the error analysis and extension to other venues, this is indeed a natural next step. The OCR and annotation challenges we encountered would interest the broader NLP and digital heritage research communities; a concise research note for an ACL or EMNLP demo/workshop could stimulate further collaborations or feedback. Sunita, I look forward to your initial structure for the error analysis, and maybe Ananya can provide guidance on which upcoming tracks (demos, workshops, or short papers) would be most receptive. It may also be strategic to position our extension as offering reusable tools/workflows for other cohort-based or multilingual historical datasets.  The idea of an online hands-on session after JCDL is excellent. As we have working scripts and demonstration assets, these could be showcased in a tutorial for early-career researchers or archivists. I suggest that Sunita and I coordinate offline to draft a tentative outline and timeline, after which we can circulate to the rest of the group for further input.  I concur that an all-hands meeting post-acceptance notification will help us synchronize both our conference preparations and subsequent research directions. Please propose your preferred windows for such a call, and we can identify a slot accommodating all time zones.  Thank you once again for your collegiality and forward-thinking perspectives. I look forward to advancing these plans together.  Best regards,  Ramesh  Prof. Ramesh Bhatia   Department of Computer Science   Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

full_email_context: Thread ID: 9JZES6 Mail ID: MAILRS58KYFJ Date: 12th October 2023 From: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> Subject: Meeting Minutes – Project Retrospective & Workflow Reference Review (11th October 2021)  Dear Sunita, Ramesh, and Michael,  Thank you all for your active participation and constructive inputs during our review meeting on 11th October 2021. As agreed, I am circulating the minutes to document our discussions, track action items, and establish a timeline for finalizing our Project Retrospective & Workflow Reference.  **Attendees:** Sunita Sen, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia, Dr. Michael Bradley, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee   **Duration:** 45 minutes  **Key Discussions and Outcomes:**  1. **Draft Outline Overview (Sunita):**    - Sunita summarized the structure and highlighted sections requiring additional detail: notably, the roles/responsibilities matrix and the template library for manuscript and correspondence formats.    - Group confirmed the outline aligns well with our objectives for both onboarding and process optimization.  2. **Visual Workflow Presentation (Michael):**    - Michael walked us through the Lucidchart flowchart, explaining key coordination points and escalation triggers. Group agreed the legend enhances clarity, and the distinction between journal and conference pathways was praised.    - Action: Michael to incorporate feedback on handoff annotations, especially for remote collaboration scenarios.  3. **Section Feedback & Action Points:**    - Ramesh will flesh out examples of communication challenges faced when adhering to international publishing protocols and compile anonymized escalation logs.    - Ananya to contribute content on inter-institutional compliance requirements, especially UK and EU data alignment considerations.    - Sunita will integrate a checklist for periodic self-assessment at each major project milestone.  4. **Lessons Learned Summaries:**    - Discussed the effectiveness of early role allocation and the importance of proactively flagging bottlenecks.    - Recommended capturing these as a dedicated section, to aid future project onboarding and workflow standardization.  5. **Next Steps & Timelines:**    - Target date for all section revisions: 18th October 2021    - Final review meeting (proposed): 22nd October 2021    - Sunita to coordinate compilation and circulate a near-final draft for sign-off  Please let me know if there are any omissions or corrections to these minutes. Thank you again for your outstanding collaboration—looking forward to shaping a reference that will serve both our group and the broader community well.  Best wishes,  Ananya  Dr. Ananya Chatterjee   Department of Computer Science   University of Oxford

I am very encouraged by the logical flow and the range of topics covered—it provides an effective basis for both our collaborative writing and for communicating the broader impact of our work to the heritage-NLP community.  Regarding the repository, I will work with Sunita to review our scripts and annotation templates within the next week and begin drafting a README and compliance checklist to ensure that all shared materials adhere to ACM and institutional policies. I agree that the normalization methodology and the reproducibility framework deserve particular emphasis, given the significant feedback we received from JCDL participants. We might also consider including a brief “lessons for community practice” subsection, highlighting recurrent themes from attendee outreach and questions that surfaced during the tutorial Q&A.  Additionally, I recommend a short discussion of evaluation metrics for normalization—perhaps we can briefly report on token-level accuracy, edit distance, and inter-annotator agreement metrics, as these were topics of significant interest during the interactive session. I would be happy to draft this subsection based on our demo code and tutorial notes.  I agree with the timeline you suggested. A meeting after 12 August works well for me to establish writing assignments and clarify submission logistics. I will also review recent JOCCH guidelines regarding supplementary materials and open-data statements ahead of our discussion.  Looking forward to further collaboration and everyone’s thoughts on these points!  Best regards,  Michael

full_email_context: Thread ID: X7RSBS Mail ID: MAILTW5X48Z1 Date: 29th January 2020 From: Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> Subject: Input on Retrospective Review & April Scheduling  Dear Sunita, Ananya, and Ramesh,  Thank you, Sunita, for getting the ball rolling on our internal retrospective, and to Ananya for initiating this valuable process. I am likewise convinced that our documented experience with reproducibility, accessibility, and dataset normalization could serve as the foundation for both internal best practices and potential future outreach—particularly in the context of historical NLP.  Per Sunita’s suggestion, I will focus my contribution on outlining the reproducibility framework we developed, including: - Comprehensive metadata capture and version control for evolving historical corpora. - Standardized documentation templates that facilitate both internal handoffs and external audits (e.g., for journal reviewers or open data repositories). - Lessons learned regarding automating provenance tracking across text normalization and alignment pipelines.  I will aim to draft a 2-3 paragraph summary by 25 March and upload it to the shared drive alongside Sunita’s entity alignment section. I encourage discussion on whether any specific reproducibility pain points (such as file format drift or annotation disagreements) merit special treatment in a methods appendix for future submissions.  For the consolidation call, I am generally available for a 30–45 minute Google Meet session within 4–8 April. My preference would be for 6 or 7 April, early afternoon UK time (which should also be comfortable for India and the US West Coast). Please let me know if these slots are generally convenient, so Sunita can coordinate.  Finally, if we see strong alignment among our notes, I suggest we consider sketching an outline for a reproducibility or workflow best practices tutorial to target at JCDL or even a special interest group session at ACL. I’m happy to support co-authorship on any such initiative.  Looking forward to your feedback and everyone’s input.  Best regards,  Michael

full_email_context: Thread ID: X7RSBS Mail ID: MAILTW5X48Z1 Date: 29th January 2020 From: Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> Subject: Input on Retrospective Review & April Scheduling  Dear Sunita, Ananya, and Ramesh,  Thank you, Sunita, for getting the ball rolling on our internal retrospective, and to Ananya for initiating this valuable process. I am likewise convinced that our documented experience with reproducibility, accessibility, and dataset normalization could serve as the foundation for both internal best practices and potential future outreach—particularly in the context of historical NLP.  Per Sunita’s suggestion, I will focus my contribution on outlining the reproducibility framework we developed, including: - Comprehensive metadata capture and version control for evolving historical corpora. - Standardized documentation templates that facilitate both internal handoffs and external audits (e.g., for journal reviewers or open data repositories). - Lessons learned regarding automating provenance tracking across text normalization and alignment pipelines.  I will aim to draft a 2-3 paragraph summary by 25 March and upload it to the shared drive alongside Sunita’s entity alignment section. I encourage discussion on whether any specific reproducibility pain points (such as file format drift or annotation disagreements) merit special treatment in a methods appendix for future submissions.  For the consolidation call, I am generally available for a 30–45 minute Google Meet session within 4–8 April. My preference would be for 6 or 7 April, early afternoon UK time (which should also be comfortable for India and the US West Coast). Please let me know if these slots are generally convenient, so Sunita can coordinate.  Finally, if we see strong alignment among our notes, I suggest we consider sketching an outline for a reproducibility or workflow best practices tutorial to target at JCDL or even a special interest group session at ACL. I’m happy to support co-authorship on any such initiative.  Looking forward to your feedback and everyone’s input.  Best regards,  Michael

full_email_context: Thread ID: GUOAF3 Mail ID: MAILHZ4F1J3G Date: 9th November 2019 From: Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> To: Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> Subject: Final Caption for Fig. 3 & Edge Case Documentation (SUB-JOCCH-2019-0187)  Dear Ramesh, Sunita, and Ananya,  As promised, I am submitting the finalized caption for Figure 3, incorporating the team’s feedback from our 15 December meeting. The revised version more explicitly delineates the genre segmentation methodology, with clear demarcation of workflow across the Bengali and English corpora, and clarifies the edge cases noted in the supplementary “Annotator_Agreement_ByGenre” tables. I have appended a brief cross-reference statement to direct readers to specific examples of NER ambiguity (e.g., colonial administrative terms, ethnonyms differing by context) and provided a short note on the annotation policy adjustments undertaken after preliminary inter-annotator agreement analysis.  You can find the updated caption and tabular summary in our shared Drive under “Minor_Revisions > Fig3_Final_MBradley_17Dec21.docx.” Please review and let me know if further linguistic fine-tuning or formatting is required ahead of integrating with the master manuscript file. I have also included a bulleted documentation of annotation outliers to facilitate efficient reviewer response preparation.  With this, all requested minor revision tasks appear on track for internal compilation by our 20 December target. Please notify me promptly if any additional reviewer remarks need reinforcing within the caption, or if you foresee overlap with Ananya’s final ethics section amendments.  Many thanks once again for the collaborative momentum—we are nearly ready for resubmission.  Best regards,  Michael

full_email_context: Thread ID: NCXC1E Mail ID: MAIL95QLTX1E Date: 22nd July 2023 From: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in> To: Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> Subject: Availability for Rehearsal and Presenter Instructions Input (JCDL 2023)  Dear Ramesh, Ananya, and Michael,  Thank you, Ramesh, for your thoughtful reflection and for volunteering to draft the “Presenter Instructions” checklist. I fully concur that these interim weeks prior to the conference represent an invaluable opportunity to further fine-tune our live session strategy and group dynamics. A brief rehearsal dedicated to opening and closing remarks, as well as handling the audience Q&A, would indeed help us optimize for engagement and smooth delivery.  Regarding availability, I am flexible for the suggested rehearsal slots between 17–21 April. My preferred dates would be the afternoons of 18 April or 20 April (IST), but I am willing to adjust depending on what best suits everyone. Please let me know your preferences, or if there is a consensus, I will make the corresponding arrangements and circulate a calendar invite with a Zoom link.  In preparation, could we also each draft a ~90 second introductory statement reflecting our unique contributions and institutional perspectives? I am happy to coordinate these into a cohesive opening script if everyone shares their drafts by this Friday. For the closing segment, perhaps we can collectively brainstorm key takeaways emphasizing both the cross-institutional nature and the ethical imperatives of our NLP work on historical data.  Additionally, Ramesh, I’d be happy to review or augment the presenter checklist with any learnings from the current JCDL guidelines once circulated. Ananya and Michael, if either of you have experience with live session moderation at prior JCDLs, any tips or do’s and don’ts would be most welcome additions to the checklist.  Thank you all again for your commitment and collegiality. I look forward to your availability confirmations—and to collaboratively refining our session for a memorable JCDL 2023 presentation.  Best regards,  Sunita  Sunita Sen   PhD Scholar   Department of Computer Science   Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

full_email_context: Thread ID: J1FCSM Mail ID: MAILNP84KJY2 Date: 22nd February 2020 From: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> To: Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> Subject: Master Slide Deck PDF & Submission Timeline for JCDL Tutorial Proposal  Dear Ramesh, Sunita, and Michael,  Thank you all for your contributions and careful review of the integrated slide deck materials. I am pleased to report that I have now completed the assembly of the master slide deck, incorporating all finalized visuals, transitions, and our concluding discussion emphasizing workflow transferability. This version includes Sunita’s anonymized mapping samples (with schematic overlays), Michael’s FAIR pipeline summary (including the sensitivity annotation), and an updated concluding slide synthesizing our broader value proposition for multi-script historical NLP applications.  The finalized slide deck, in the required landscape PDF format (10 slides, all visuals captioned), is now available in the shared drive folder “JCDL2020_Tutorial_Proposal” as “Master_Slide_Deck_JCDL2020_Final_19Apr2020.pdf”. Please review the document at your earliest convenience, focusing particularly on the narrative flow, clarity of graphics, and the highlighted reviewer guidelines in the appendix slide. If there are any minor corrections, typographical issues, or suggestions for last-minute polish, do let me know before 21:00 UK time tonight, as I intend to proceed with the formal submission to the JCDL 2020 committee immediately thereafter.  Once all of you confirm your approval, I will submit the proposal via the conference portal and circulate the submission receipt and tracking ID to the group for our records.  Many thanks again for your collaborative spirit and attention to detail throughout this preparation phase. I am optimistic that our collective efforts will be well received by the JCDL tutorial selection committee.  Looking forward to your confirmations.  Best regards,  Ananya

evidence_sentence: I am writing to share a draft of the scenario annotation addressing stakeholder engagement strategies for non-English-speaking press teams, as requested by Reviewer 2.
full_email_context: Thread ID: K241SL Mail ID: MAILA7U5J2LF Date: 22nd July 2022 From: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> Subject: Draft of Non-English Press Stakeholder Engagement – Section 4 Annotation  Dear Sunita, Ramesh, and Michael,  Thank you, Michael, for your clear task allocations and for summarizing our next steps toward the camera-ready JCDL submission. Congratulations once again to the entire team for reaching this important milestone!  I am writing to share a draft of the scenario annotation addressing stakeholder engagement strategies for non-English-speaking press teams, as requested by Reviewer 2. I have attached a proposed text intended for insertion in Section 4 (“Illustrative Metadata Disclosure Use-Cases”) following the UK regional example. This annotation draws on recent casework in both India and the European Union, highlighting protocols for engaging local-language press offices and referencing our experience with translated embargo communications.  Draft annotation:  *“Scenario: Regional Media – In instances where a press office operates primarily in a non-English language (e.g., Hindi for RTI disclosures in India or Italian for EU cultural heritage projects), the compliance team provides translated embargo statements, coordinates bilingual FAQ dissemination, and, where possible, designates a local liaison to facilitate queries. For high-visibility releases, legal documentation and protocol summaries are adapted in collaboration with in-country press and legal advisors to ensure clarity and jurisdictional fidelity.”*  Please review and suggest edits to tailor the example more closely to our annex’s existing style or to align with your own institutional experience (especially Ramesh, your insights on Indian press engagement would be helpful). As discussed, I wanted to promptly follow up regarding the outstanding legal framework materials and clarify the relevant Data Protection Bill clauses for embedding in our corpus methodology and annotation guidance.  **Legal Protocol Matrix Draft:**   By this Sunday (5 November), I will upload to the shared drive a detailed comparative matrix of current data-sharing and archival annotation protocols. This will feature: - Side-by-side comparison of the latest amendments to the India Data Protection Bill (2022) with those from the EU and UK (esp. GDPR and local heritage exceptions). - Annotations on researcher responsibilities, particularly regarding third-party historical data, anonymization policies, and cross-regional archival consent. - Highlighted subclauses on annotation, focusing on sections (Sec. 37B & Sec. 45C) recently introduced, which pertain to explicit subject consent and retention for cultural datasets.  **For manuscript integration:**   Sunita, you are welcome to cite the aforementioned sections (with Bill text excerpts) as footnotes in the methodology, alongside a summary paragraph for the main text and extended context in the appendix as discussed with Ananya. I will also provide brief legal notes on compliance overlap and potential ambiguities, should reviewers request further clarification.  **Action Points Recap for Legal Contributions:** - Upload protocol matrix by 5 November. - Circulate concise legal footnotes and summary text to Sunita and Ananya for integration/review by 8 November. - Coordinate with Ananya next week for the final visual layout of the legal comparative table (including both tabular and narrative elements for the appendix).  Please let me know if you envision any changes to the format or if there are other cross-country clauses either Michael or Ananya would like incorporated. Looking forward to tightening this critical aspect of our revision and ensuring compliance clarity throughout.  Best regards,  Ramesh  Prof. Ramesh Bhatia   Department of Computer Science   Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

full_email_context: Thread ID: RYT897 Mail ID: MAIL6SKZ4RXV Date: 23rd September 2022 From: Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> Subject: Post-Submission Plan: Dissemination and Future Directions  Dear all,  Now that JCDL 2022 has officially acknowledged receipt of our submission (SUB-JCDL-2022-1189), I would like to propose we take stock of next steps—both for maximizing the visibility of our conference contribution and for planning possible follow-up publications or collaborative expansion.  A few key suggestions for discussion:  1. Dissemination ahead of JCDL: With the embargo periods and conference copyright rules in mind, would it be permissible to share a lightly redacted preprint, or perhaps a blog post summarizing our findings for a wider audience (e.g., AI and digital humanities outreach platforms)? Sunita, do you have insights from previous IACS experience with such dissemination? I’d be happy to provide a draft if the group is interested. 2. Roadmap for Extension: Our current presentation focuses on data-driven cross-lingual pipelines, primarily for archival document alignment and annotation. There seems to be real appetite in the community for follow-up on error analysis (especially with OCR artifacts and low-resource scripts). Perhaps we can outline a brief research note or demo for submission to a later venue (ACL system demonstrations or EMNLP workshops)? 3. Collaborative Workshops: Given that we now have a technically robust, accessibility-compliant workflow, and broad team expertise, would you be interested in organizing a hands-on tutorial or community code sprint (remotely) after JCDL? This could help us build relationships for future grant applications. 4. Next Meeting: Should we schedule a brief team call post-acceptance notification (early June) to plan our JCDL attendance (in-person/virtual) and related outreach activities?  Looking forward to hearing your thoughts on dissemination strategies and next steps. Please indicate your preferences, and let me know if you foresee any logistical or compliance constraints.  Congratulations once again to everyone for our successful, smooth submission. I am genuinely excited about what we can accomplish as a team moving forward.  Best regards,  Michael  Dr. Michael Bradley   Department of Computer Science   Stanford University

full_email_context: Thread ID: 35LJ47 Mail ID: MAILY2TUEXC9 Date: 21st August 2023 From: Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> To: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in> Subject: Portal Access Confirmed & Suggestions for Potential Reviewers  Dear Ananya, Ramesh, and Sunita,  Thank you for keeping us apprised of the submission progress and the expected editorial review timeline. I confirm that I have successfully accessed the ACM JOCCH submission portal using the co-author invitation—both the manuscript and all supplementary materials appear correctly linked and visible from my account.  Regarding potential reviewers, I have carefully considered scholars with relevant expertise in both historical NLP pipelines and semantic evaluation frameworks, while ensuring none are directly affiliated with our current or recent projects to avoid conflicts of interest. My initial recommendations are as follows:  1. Dr. Lisa Nguyen (University of Washington) – Her work on entity linking methods for digitized archival texts aligns closely with our schema and adjudication processes. 2. Prof. Arvind Narayanan (IIT Delhi) – His research on multilingual heritage corpora and error propagation in annotation could add valuable perspective, particularly to our treatment of Bengali legal documents. 3. Dr. Claudia Ricci (University of Bologna) – Speciality in computational methods for historical legal corpora; her recent publications address issues of annotation consistency and adjudication that dovetail with our approach.  I will forward these suggestions to you confidentially as per the editorial request. If anyone would like to propose alternative reviewers or has concerns about those listed above, please let me know by the 25 May internal deadline. I also second Ananya’s suggestion to prepare our author contribution statements proactively—I’ve started drafting mine (with a focus on methodology and data curation, in line with the CRediT taxonomy) and will circulate it for your review.  Great job to everyone on the final integration and submission logistics. Please alert the group if any updates arise or if further materials are needed before editorial review is complete.  Best regards,  Michael  Dr. Michael Bradley   Department of Computer Science   Stanford University

full_email_context: Thread ID: 35LJ47 Mail ID: MAILY2TUEXC9 Date: 21st August 2023 From: Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> To: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in> Subject: Portal Access Confirmed & Suggestions for Potential Reviewers  Dear Ananya, Ramesh, and Sunita,  Thank you for keeping us apprised of the submission progress and the expected editorial review timeline. I confirm that I have successfully accessed the ACM JOCCH submission portal using the co-author invitation—both the manuscript and all supplementary materials appear correctly linked and visible from my account.  Regarding potential reviewers, I have carefully considered scholars with relevant expertise in both historical NLP pipelines and semantic evaluation frameworks, while ensuring none are directly affiliated with our current or recent projects to avoid conflicts of interest. My initial recommendations are as follows:  1. Dr. Lisa Nguyen (University of Washington) – Her work on entity linking methods for digitized archival texts aligns closely with our schema and adjudication processes. 2. Prof. Arvind Narayanan (IIT Delhi) – His research on multilingual heritage corpora and error propagation in annotation could add valuable perspective, particularly to our treatment of Bengali legal documents. 3. Dr. Claudia Ricci (University of Bologna) – Speciality in computational methods for historical legal corpora; her recent publications address issues of annotation consistency and adjudication that dovetail with our approach.  I will forward these suggestions to you confidentially as per the editorial request. If anyone would like to propose alternative reviewers or has concerns about those listed above, please let me know by the 25 May internal deadline. I also second Ananya’s suggestion to prepare our author contribution statements proactively—I’ve started drafting mine (with a focus on methodology and data curation, in line with the CRediT taxonomy) and will circulate it for your review.  Great job to everyone on the final integration and submission logistics. Please alert the group if any updates arise or if further materials are needed before editorial review is complete.  Best regards,  Michael  Dr. Michael Bradley   Department of Computer Science   Stanford University

Consolidated quotes from Dr. Ananya Chatterjee and Oxford’s principal investigator, focused on technical innovation and cross-institutional partnership. 2. Summary statements from Prof. Ramesh Bhatia, emphasizing the societal impact and outreach dimensions of our project, with particular reference to multilingual accessibility and heritage preservation. 3. Visual materials curated by Dr. Michael Bradley and the Stanford team, including (a) a schematic of our language model domain adaptation workflow and (b) an infographic summarizing joint publication and media impact metrics. 4. Brief introductory blurbs and background information from both Oxford and IACS, tailored to suit conference audience requirements.  All submitted materials have undergone internal review and are fully cleared by our respective communications offices for inclusion in JCDL’s official newsletter and promotional features. If you require alternative formatting, or if specific asset resolutions are preferred, please advise and we will provide revised versions promptly.  We look forward to the release of the newsletter and are prepared to coordinate any supplementary content or institutional quotes as needed in the forthcoming days. Please inform us when the draft bulletin is available for review ahead of publication, or if further clarifications are needed from any team member.  Thank you for your ongoing collaboration and for supporting the visibility of our NLP on historical data project within the JCDL community.  Best regards,  Sunita  Sunita Sen   PhD Scholar   Department of Computer Science   Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

full_email_context: Thread ID: JOFJ6E Mail ID: MAIL6J5HV9QT Date: 14th October 2022 From: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> Subject: Accessibility Final Verification & Contingency Preparation Update  Dear Sunita, Ramesh, and Michael,  Thank you, Sunita, for preparing the supplemental PDF NER guide with updated accessibility features and alerting us so promptly after upload. I have now tested the file extensively with Mac OS VoiceOver and JAWS for Windows and am pleased to report that navigation, alt text, and reading order work efficiently on both platforms. The logical headings and visual descriptions perform as intended, facilitating clear step-by-step annotation review. At this time, no further adjustments are necessary for the screen reader-specific content, but I will keep an eye out for any feedback from participants who rely on other assistive technologies.  Ramesh, I appreciate your quick integration of Michael’s multilingual annotation FAQ updates into the breakout packet. Sunita, thank you also for logging participant queries into the “Inquiries” doc—having early visibility into questions about dataset citation and session timing will be invaluable for our opening remarks and initial Q&A.  Regarding contingency preparations, Sunita’s progress on the emergency email template and backup datasets is much appreciated. Once shared, I would be happy to review and suggest any additional clarifications that may ease stress for participants in the moment. Michael, your ongoing input on technical troubleshooting steps (especially for North American time zones and browser-specific issues) will further strengthen our contingency resources.  If there are no objections, I propose we convene a brief check-in call on 24 May, at 16:00 BST / 20:30 IST / 8:00 PDT, to finalize outstanding items and rehearse the contingency communications protocol together. Please confirm availability at your earliest convenience, and feel free to propose an alternative if this time is inconvenient.  Thank you again for your collective diligence and teamwork as we approach the event’s final phase.  Best wishes,  Ananya  Dr. Ananya Chatterjee   Department of Computer Science   University of Oxford

object_label: prepare and share revised compliance appendix draft and comprehensive attribution table
evidence_sentence: Thank you, Ramesh, for preparing and sharing the revised compliance appendix draft and the comprehensive attribution table.
full_email_context: Thread ID: GGM0ZF Mail ID: MAIL89WJ3NCP Date: 11th August 2019 From: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> To: Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> Subject: Re: Compliance Appendix Revision Review, Licensing Alignment & Next Steps (SUB-JOCCH-2019-0187)  Dear Ramesh, Sunita, and Michael,  Thank you, Ramesh, for preparing and sharing the revised compliance appendix draft and the comprehensive attribution table. I have now reviewed the document with special focus on the articulation of open licenses, licensing attributions for each archive, and the explicit separation between CC BY 4.0-licensed annotations and source scans governed by parental institutional policies.  From the perspective of current European library practices, and following the latest guidance from the Oxford Bodleian Digital Collections Team, I can confirm that your drafted content aligns well with best practices. Explicitly referencing institutional license statements and including direct hyperlinks for source verification is strongly encouraged. Your clarification note on “derivative use” is also a welcome addition, as it precludes common misunderstandings about re-use boundaries. I have made a few minor wording suggestions in the shared doc to strengthen these points and clarify that users of any annotated or processed derivative must check original archive terms for any non-annotation data redistribution.  Sunita, as soon as Ramesh signs off on these small edits, you should integrate this compliance appendix version into the main manuscript. Please also update the response letter to include specific mention of our appended compliance mapping table and the improved clarity around third-party reuse.  Michael, the clarification you suggested in your earlier email regarding annotator rights is now reflected in the disclaimer section—I appreciate your attention to precise language about data provenance and user obligations.  If everyone is in agreement, let’s aim to complete manuscript integration and finalize internal review by 7 September as planned. Please let me know if any further input is required from the Oxford side regarding licensing or best practices documentation.  Thank you all again for your dedicated and collaborative approach.  Best regards,  Ananya

full_email_context: Thread ID: WFB93D Mail ID: MAIL2XNC51SK Date: 25th January 2021 From: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in> To: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> Subject: Next Steps for Camera-Ready Submission - Clarification Tasks (SUB-JOCCH-2020-0047)  Dear Ananya, Michael, and Ramesh,  Congratulations to everyone on the conditional acceptance of our JOCCH manuscript (SUB-JOCCH-2020-0047)! I am delighted by the reviewers’ endorsement and want to express my appreciation for everyone’s contributions to reaching this stage. The outlined minor clarifications appear manageable within our current documentation structure, but I would like to propose a coordinated plan to efficiently address each point before the 16 June camera-ready deadline.  **Action Plan for Clarifications:** 1. **Recent Cross-Domain Corpus References:**      Michael, as you previously compiled the comparative tables, could you source two recent (post-2019) cross-domain historical corpora that align with our dataset inclusion criteria? Please draft concise citations and one explanatory sentence each for integration into the Methods section. Ramesh, it would be helpful if you could quickly review and sign off on these additions for completeness.  2. **“Boundary Error” Footnote for Table 2:**      Ananya, if you are able, could you suggest a succinct but explicit footnote definition for “Boundary Error” that prioritizes reader accessibility? Once you circulate the proposed text, I will insert it in the appropriate LaTeX environment and verify rendering consistency.  3. **Supplementary Notebook Intro Update:**      I am happy to revise the introductory markdown cell of the Jupyter notebook to reference the compliance protocol and attached flowchart directly. Once these edits are live, I’ll share a preview so all can confirm the update.  **Timeline:**   If possible, let’s aim to circulate initial drafts of these changes in the “CameraReady_JOCCH_Revision” shared folder by 28 May. This gives us a full two weeks for review, final integration, and technical checks in advance of the ScholarOne submission.  Please feel free to suggest alternative arrangements, or notify me in case of known scheduling conflicts that might affect these internal deadlines.  Once again, congratulations to all for your dedication and expertise through every phase of this project. Looking forward to everyone’s inputs and to completing this final step.  Best regards,  Sunita

full_email_context: Thread ID: 00OT3M Mail ID: MAIL9VY4MHG2 Date: 25th March 2025 From: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> To: Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> Subject: Re: Final Review Synthesis & Next Steps Before Colloquium Submission  Dear Ramesh, Sunita, and Michael,  Thank you, Ramesh, for your prompt synthesis of the memo and your valuable editorial refinements to the Executive Summary and conclusion. I have conducted a last detailed read-through of the final document and can confirm my full approval, both of the “Lessons Learned” content and the colloquium abstract version. The bridging language in the best practices section has improved the overall flow and highlighted the unique value each of our institutional approaches has contributed to the project.  I am also pleased with the authorship order and am happy to formally co-sign the colloquium abstract as discussed. Sunita, your draft encompasses both the technical rigor and the process insights we set out to communicate—I do not see any further required changes and endorse moving ahead as planned with the submission on 2 April.  Regarding future dissemination, I fully agree that our workflow solutions—specifically the version management schema and feedback cycle matrix—could form the basis for a compelling short-form or methods paper. I suggest we start outlining such a piece post-colloquium, potentially targeting EMNLP System Demonstrations or the JDoc Technical Communication section as strong options. We can revisit this after receiving feedback from the colloquium committee and possibly integrate any pertinent questions from the audience into our manuscript as a demonstration of broader community relevance.  Thank you all once more for the collaborative precision and goodwill throughout this process. I will monitor the inbox for further comments before the final lock-in/Ramesh’s archive tomorrow at 09:00 IST. Wishing everyone a productive start to April and looking forward to the next steps together.  Best regards,  Ananya  Dr. Ananya Chatterjee   Department of Computer Science   University of Oxford

Sunita, your illustrative use-case insert has been seamlessly integrated, and I have restyled the protocol section as agreed, with all track changes from Ramesh and language clarifications now incorporated and accepted. Assuming approval, I will draft a brief cover letter reflecting our institutional compliance and multi-regional cooperation for Sunita’s signature.  Looking forward to a productive and conclusive session.  Best wishes,  Ananya  Dr. Ananya Chatterjee   Department of Computer Science   University of Oxford
