full_email_context: Thread ID: N0EBZ1 Mail ID: MAILS58JG2LU Date: 19th December 2020 From: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in> To: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> Subject: Final Review and Checklist for JOCCH Minor Revision Resubmission  Dear Ananya, Michael, and Ramesh,  Thank you, Ramesh, for finalizing and promptly uploading the compliance protocol documentation and flowchart. I have reviewed both the narrative section and the visual schematic, and they are comprehensive and precisely aligned with the recommendations from Reviewer 2. The explicit cross-referencing to data retention and anonymization policies not only satisfies mandatory journal requirements but also greatly improves the clarity for future readers and replicators of our workflow.  As we approach our internal review session on 7 April, I would like to suggest that we conduct a systematic check of the full revision package, leveraging the following checklist:  1. **Integration**: Confirm that all updated sections (compliance, response letter, supplementary notebook, and reformatted Table 2) are harmoniously integrated and correctly referenced between the main manuscript and appendices. 2. **Rebuttal Letter**: Ensure each reviewer comment is addressed transparently with direct links to the revised content, using the original reviewer numbering for traceability. 3. **Formatting Consistency**: Verify that our LaTeX-generated figures, tables, and cross-references are stable across PDF viewers and adhere to JOCCH’s latest formatting guidelines. 4. **Supplementary Files**: Double-check file naming conventions and completeness in the ScholarOne upload folder to avoid submission errors. 5. **Cover Letter**: Review the cover letter draft for conciseness, clarity, and proper declaration statements, especially with respect to prior publication and data transparency.  If possible, could everyone add brief comments directly in the FinalDraft_02Apr folder checklist by the end of 7 April, indicating any remaining concerns or explicit approval of the package? Ananya, once all confirmations are received, please proceed with finalizing the ScholarOne upload and notify us so we can monitor for successful submission and any system correspondence.  Thank you all for your diligence throughout this revision phase. I am optimistic about a strong response from the editorial board.  Best regards,  Sunita

full_email_context: Thread ID: 4X69T3 Mail ID: MAILP4J2S6XC Date: 8th August 2022 From: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in> To: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> Subject: IACS Press Office Submission Confirmation – Next Steps  Dear Ananya, Ramesh, and Michael,  Thank you very much, Ananya, for circulating the finalized draft and managing the integration of all institutional feedback so seamlessly. I wanted to inform the group that as of this morning, the finalized press release file (“JCDL2022_Press_Release_Final.docx”) has been uploaded and formally submitted to the IACS Press and Public Relations Office, following the standard workflow. I have ensured to cite all co-authors, include accurate project and funding attributions, and reference the embargo and distribution protocols as specified in our template. Confirmation of receipt has already been acknowledged by Ms. Nanda Roy, the Communications Coordinator at IACS, and the file is now under internal review.  To keep everyone updated on next steps: - The press office aims to finalize compliance and factual vetting within 2–3 business days. - Pending their sign-off and any minor factual queries, I will notify the group of official approval or required edits. - I would encourage Michael and Ananya to similarly confirm formal submission to their respective communications/press teams to ensure parallel progress. - Once all institutional approvals are in place, I’ll coordinate with you on a synchronized, embargo-respecting release, targeting the JCDL program publication window in alignment with the committee’s timetable.  Please let me know as soon as your institutional teams confirm receipt so we can keep the process coordinated. If there are any last-minute adjustments or additional documentation requested from IACS or either partner office, kindly cc the group so we maintain alignment.  Thank you again for the outstanding collective effort. I am very much looking forward to sharing our work with the broader public and academic community.  Best regards,  Sunita  Sunita Sen   PhD Scholar   Department of Computer Science   Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

We will notify you of any required further action, or when a decision is made.  No further action is presently required from the author team. In the interim, should you have any questions regarding reviewer anonymity, data sharing, or wish to update contact information, please contact us at editorial@jocch.acm.org and quote your submission ID (SUB-JOCCH-2019-0187) in all correspondence.  Thank you for choosing the ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage for your work. We look forward to being in touch once the next stage of the review process is completed.  Best regards,  The JOCCH Editorial Office   ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage

Many thanks to Sunita for leading the submission and to each of you for your ongoing attention to detail throughout this process. Your expertise on regional press protocols will be invaluable for contextualizing media engagement in multilingual contexts (e.g., including a brief example reference for regional Indian or European outlets).  2. **Typographical Corrections**: Ramesh, would you review Section 2.3 and the version changelog appendix for the minor typographical issues highlighted in the reviewer attachments? If repository access is needed, let me know and I can coordinate with the Stanford library team for suitable link-outs.  Once draft changes are circulated, I recommend a consolidated walkthrough (Google Doc comments and tracked changes) by 19 February, with a short group call or asynchronous sign-off prior to upload. Please signal any foreseen schedule constraints or suggest alternative approaches.  Thank you all again for your exceptional collegiality and commitment to rigor in cross-border research documentation!  Best, Michael  Dr. Michael Bradley   Department of Computer Science   Stanford University

full_email_context: Thread ID: YRDRSO Mail ID: MAILWQ3E1F7V Date: 3rd June 2021 From: Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> Subject: IACS Policy Review: Embargo Note Finalization and Compliance Integration  Dear Sunita, Ananya, and Michael,  Thank you for your prompt updates on Overleaf and for the exemplary cross-institutional synthesis of compliance and evaluation protocols. I have now completed my detailed review of the revised IACS embargo and release note within the Supplementary Materials/Compliance section. Sunita, your latest clarifications, especially the refined articulation of time-bounded embargo and transparent release conditions, fully align with both IACS policy and the referenced UKRI/Stanford frameworks Ananya annotated. The incorporation of explicit, reviewer-facing assurances and synthetic preview sample protocol also reflects best practices as informed by recent ACL resource track guidelines.  I have left minor editorial feedback directly in Overleaf (chiefly clarifying the timing for embargo expiration notifications and reiterating eligibility criteria for restricted data access). No substantive content changes are needed at this stage—the underlying compliance structure and narrative logic are robust and should satisfy both institutional and conference scrutiny.  Given the nearing 18 October internal review milestone, I support Sunita’s suggestion for a final integrated read-through once her ongoing edits to the Results and Acknowledgments are complete. Michael, perhaps you could coordinate a brief 30-minute Zoom session on 19 October to review harmonized compliance language and resolve any lingering points ahead of formal manuscript circulation? If this works for all, please share a proposed time and meeting link.  Thank you all again for your impressive diligence and collegiality—our manuscript is notably strengthened by this rigorous coordination.  Best regards,  Ramesh Bhatia   Professor, Department of Computer Science   Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

As promised, I am sharing the draft Oxford press note in the shared folder (“JCDL2022_SpotlightPrep”) as of this morning. The draft draws on the key themes we discussed: the significance of cross-institution protocols for multilingual NLP, the NDAI integration use case, and our broader impact on responsible model development for cultural heritage applications. Please review the document at your convenience—I invite your suggestions on phrasing or content, particularly any institutional highlights or technical results you feel we should further emphasize for clarity and outreach resonance. Sunita, I trust this draft will align well with your IACS press messaging; let’s coordinate further to ensure consistency in timing and tone.  Regarding the rehearsal: Thank you, Ramesh, for suggesting 8 and 9 April as potential windows. I am available for a 30–40 minute session on 8 April between 10:00–12:00 GMT. Michael, could you please confirm your preference within this window, or let us know if an adjacent time would work better? Sunita, does this slot suit you as well? Once all have confirmed, I will circulate the Zoom invite and a rehearsal agenda so we can address flows, transitions, and any last-minute adjustments.  Finally, a gentle reminder: If there are any outstanding slide updates (including the NDAI user feedback summary or late-stage infographics), please upload them to the shared drive by end of day on 6 April. This will grant everyone sufficient time for review and ensure that our dry run reflects the finalized content.  Thank you again for your commitment and timely communication. I look forward to your feedback on the press note and to joining you all for a productive rehearsal next week.  Best regards,  Ananya  Dr. Ananya Chatterjee   Department of Computer Science   University of Oxford

I am energized by our shared vision for expanding the work, and I appreciate your decisive responses on both the direction for a journal extension and the outreach roadmap.  Ramesh, I will prepare and share supplementary annotation logs and all relevant annotation metadata by early next week. This will include: - The full annotator activity logs (with timestamped actions), - Additional meta-annotations on language variety and script conventions, - Inter-annotator commentaries collected during conflict resolution rounds, and - The batch of normalization edge cases that may be useful in the guidelines section.  Ananya, I’m happy to coordinate with you as you draft the normalization and inter-annotator agreement sections. Please let me know if you need me to process any comparative statistics or generate plots—otherwise, I’ll upload the data to our shared repository and highlight key segments that seem most relevant for extension.  Michael, I look forward to your preliminary table comparing resource hosting venues and appreciate your offer to coordinate the dataset note logistics. If you have a template or format in mind for the user study survey, please circulate it so I can help refine questions related to usability and linguistic diversity.  Additionally, could we consider adding a preliminary timeline for both the journal submission and resource paper, based on the preferred venues’ review windows? This will help us distribute writing and revision tasks more evenly after the 24 April call.   Many thanks to everyone for maintaining our momentum and camaraderie post-ACL. Please let me know if there are other materials, analyses, or datasets I can assemble prior to the planning meeting.  Looking forward to our next steps!  Warm regards,  Sunita  Sunita Sen   PhD Scholar   Department of Computer Science   Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

object_label: finalizing the evaluation metrics narrative
evidence_sentence: I wanted to update you all on the progress with the evaluation metrics narrative and compliance annotations.
full_email_context: Thread ID: NL6U5C Mail ID: MAILT2K1X8QP Date: 31st May 2021 From: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> Subject: Drafted Evaluation Metrics Narrative and Overleaf Annotations  Dear Sunita, Michael, and Ramesh,  Following the productive discussion during our 12 October coordination meeting and the subsequent distribution of minutes and action points, I wanted to update you all on the progress with the evaluation metrics narrative and compliance annotations.  I have completed an initial draft of the rationale for our hybrid evaluation framework, with particular emphasis on our dual use of quantitative metrics (F1, precision, recall) and qualitative expert assessments of ambiguous or context-dependent historical language phenomena. The text aims to directly address the updated ACL resource track guidelines, showcasing how our choice explicitly supports both reproducibility and scholarly depth. I have uploaded the draft to the “Evaluation Framework” section in Overleaf and provided in-line references to the relevant ACL reproducibility checklist guidance.  Additionally, I have annotated the dual-archiving and embargo protocol segments, drawing on both the Oxford/UKRI and Stanford Humanities best-practice documents. These Overleaf comments highlight reviewer-facing language and flag potential queries—especially about synthetic data previews for restricted access corpora, as discussed in our meeting. Sunita, your embargo process note aligns well with the UKRI model; I have suggested a sentence or two that can further clarify time-bound release assurances. Ramesh, please let me know if these annotations appropriately reflect both the IACS and global compliance expectations, or if additional tailoring is necessary before your policy review.  Michael, I have also referenced some recent ACL artifact evaluation reviewer feedback (from 2020 resource papers) that we might consider preemptively addressing in the revised Impact and Supplementary sections.  Please review the updated content and comments in Overleaf at your earliest convenience. Feedback on clarity, coverage, or further integration with our main manuscript is most welcome as we approach our 18 October target for internal review.  Thanks again to everyone for the excellent cross-institutional coordination and feedback loops.  Best wishes,  Ananya Chatterjee   Department of Computer Science   University of Oxford

full_email_context: Thread ID: Y0UJSL Mail ID: MAILS3K7U1XC Date: 20th July 2022 From: JCDL 2022 Program Office <submissions@jcdl-conf.org> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in> CC: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> Subject: Decision Notification for JCDL 2022 Submission – SUB-JCDL-2022-0432  Dear Sunita Sen and Research Team,  We are pleased to inform you that after thorough peer review, your submission to JCDL 2022 entitled “Cross-Institutional Protocols for Metadata and Embargo: An Integrated FAQ Annex” (Submission ID: SUB-JCDL-2022-0432) has been accepted **with minor revisions**.  Reviewer feedback commended the clarity and practicality of your multi-institutional FAQ annex, particularly emphasizing the value of your illustrative metadata scenarios and the thorough attention to cross-jurisdictional policy alignment. A small number of suggestions were raised for your consideration in the camera-ready version:  1. Clarification requested regarding stakeholder engagement strategies for non-English-speaking press teams—please add one or two brief scenario annotations addressing this context. 2. Minor typographical corrections flagged in Section 2.3 and the version changelog appendix. 3. Reviewers requested that you explicitly reference the supporting documentation for regional legal exceptions (especially RTI and FERPA cases), with appropriate hyperlinks or appendices if possible.  You will find detailed reviewer comments and guidance attached.  **Next Steps:**   - Please prepare a revised camera-ready version addressing the points above.   - The camera-ready deadline for JCDL 2022 is **2nd August 2020**. Instructions for uploading your final files will follow in a separate email.   - Should you require clarification or wish to discuss any reviewer comments, feel free to contact us at submissions@jcdl-conf.org, referencing your Submission ID.  Congratulations on reaching this important milestone. We look forward to including your work in the JCDL 2022 program and to your continued contribution to the digital libraries and cultural heritage community.  Best Regards,  JCDL 2022 Program Office   submissions@jcdl-conf.org

full_email_context: Thread ID: 81TWVD Mail ID: MAILE8G5NZ0R Date: 12th April 2021 From: Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> To: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> Subject: Stanford Media Office Process & Webinar Slide Deck Draft Timeline  Dear Ananya, Sunita, and Ramesh,  Thank you, Ananya, for outlining Oxford’s media release workflow. That transparency is extremely helpful for organizing our cross-institutional outreach. Sunita, thanks also to you for taking such steady leadership on both the IACS communications and all logistical fronts for our webinar.  To clarify Stanford’s process: our Office of University Communications (OUC) similarly requires at least 2 business days for review of any press statements referencing Stanford-affiliated researchers or institutional partnerships. Additionally, all materials must include (a) Stanford’s preferred department naming conventions, (b) a disclosure regarding the open-access nature of our work, and (c) an explicit mention of digital preservation and reproducibility priorities. I am attaching our standard OA statement and digital stewardship language to this email for reference; please feel free to adapt or request edits for alignment with your institution’s messaging.  Once the DOI and official online publication date are confirmed, please send me the finalized release materials. I will initiate the OUC’s internal review and keep you updated on their feedback or required changes. Sunita, if you need any additional compliance forms or data management assurances from the Stanford side for the IACS or webinar setups, just let me know.  On the webinar front: I am on track to share the draft slide deck framework with you all by 20 August, as agreed during our last meeting. This will include (1) an outline for my 20-min technical demo, (2) placeholders for Sunita’s introduction and for Ramesh/Ananya’s case studies, and (3) suggested visual and annotation formats for clarity across a diverse digital humanities audience. Please feel free to comment directly on the slides or suggest additional sections as needed.  Looking forward to keeping this momentum as we approach both the publication milestone and public engagement phase.  Best wishes,  Michael Bradley Assistant Professor, Department of Computer Science Stanford University michael@cs.stanford.edu

Please find below a summary of our discussion and agreed-upon action points:  **Attendees:** Ananya, Sunita, Michael, Ramesh  **1. Task Updates (as reported):** - **Compliance Protocols:** Ramesh confirmed preparation of a detailed flowchart and extended narrative covering anonymization, data retention duration (per IACS and JOCCH policy), and secure destruction protocols. Draft to be circulated by 30 March for group input. - **Supplementary Notebook:** Michael provided an overview of added markdown cells, particularly those highlighting edge case handling (low-resource, OCR noise). Integration of Sunita's sample outputs is in progress, with final notebook upload targeted for 1 April. - **Table 2 Formatting:** Sunita reported substantial progress using LaTeX adjustments and preflight PDF checks. She will seek support if persistent style discrepancies are identified and will share preview PDFs for team review. - **Response Letter:** Ananya is proactively mapping reviewer requests to manuscript locations and will update the working document as contributions are received.  **2. Technical Concerns:** - Minor LaTeX-to-Word compatibility issues remain under watch. - Cross-referencing compliance information between manuscript and notebook was agreed as necessary; Michael and Ramesh to align on reference language after both sections are drafted.  **3. Timeline and Next Steps:** - All draft revisions are expected to be ready for team review by 2 April. - Ananya will circulate the draft rebuttal and updated cover letter for final input by 5 April. - Aim to complete a consolidated final submission by 10 April, allowing a buffer for ScholarOne technicalities.  **4. Outstanding Questions:** - No unresolved action items; all members reported clear paths forward and confirmed next check-in via shared tracker.  Thank you all for your engagement and transparent communication. Please notify the group promptly if any obstacles arise, so we can maintain momentum toward resubmission.  Best regards,  Ramesh

Please find below a summary of our discussion and agreed-upon action points:  **Attendees:** Ananya, Sunita, Michael, Ramesh  **1. Task Updates (as reported):** - **Compliance Protocols:** Ramesh confirmed preparation of a detailed flowchart and extended narrative covering anonymization, data retention duration (per IACS and JOCCH policy), and secure destruction protocols. Draft to be circulated by 30 March for group input. - **Supplementary Notebook:** Michael provided an overview of added markdown cells, particularly those highlighting edge case handling (low-resource, OCR noise). Integration of Sunita's sample outputs is in progress, with final notebook upload targeted for 1 April. - **Table 2 Formatting:** Sunita reported substantial progress using LaTeX adjustments and preflight PDF checks. Technical Concerns:** - Minor LaTeX-to-Word compatibility issues remain under watch. - Cross-referencing compliance information between manuscript and notebook was agreed as necessary; Michael and Ramesh to align on reference language after both sections are drafted.  **3. Timeline and Next Steps:** - All draft revisions are expected to be ready for team review by 2 April. - Ananya will circulate the draft rebuttal and updated cover letter for final input by 5 April. - Aim to complete a consolidated final submission by 10 April, allowing a buffer for ScholarOne technicalities.  **4. Outstanding Questions:** - No unresolved action items; all members reported clear paths forward and confirmed next check-in via shared tracker.  Thank you all for your engagement and transparent communication. Please notify the group promptly if any obstacles arise, so we can maintain momentum toward resubmission.  Best regards,  Ramesh

full_email_context: Thread ID: 2D7KJK Mail ID: MAIL3JX7T2SA Date: 14th October 2024 From: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in> To: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> Subject: Submission Venue Decision & Consolidated Feedback Review Meeting  Dear Ananya, Michael, and Ramesh,  Thank you all for the exceptionally prompt and substantive feedback on the integrated technical note draft. Ananya, I appreciate your annotated tracked-changes comments—your scrutiny of the legal structures, terminological harmonization, and shifting institutional narratives was particularly helpful, and I agree with your recommendations for clarifying the archival MOU procedures in Sections 2.2 and 4.2. Michael, your “lessons learned” draft (both for the appendix and prospective blog post) offers a clear, actionable synthesis, and Ramesh, your recent clarifications around anonymized negotiation workflows and cross-archival consent are now woven throughout the compliance vignette sections.  To efficiently steer our manuscript to completion and agree on a final submission venue, I propose we hold a brief consolidation meeting on 25 September (tomorrow), aiming for a 16:30 IST / 12:00 BST / 04:00 PDT slot. I recommend a focused agenda:  1. Rapid consolidation of all outstanding revisions, cross-referencing Ananya’s and Michael's notes. 2. Venue decision: JOCCH journal (greater length/flexibility, but longer review time) vs. JCDL conference (shorter timeline, but stricter page limit) per our comparative matrix. 3. Timeline confirmation for final manuscript, figures, and supplementary appendix submission. 4. Planning for a parallel blog post or public preprint if consensus favors.  Please confirm your availability for this time, or if adjustment is needed, suggest nearby alternatives. I will circulate an annotated summary of required revisions by tonight, so we may enter our meeting fully prepared to finalize.  Many thanks, again, to each of you for your rigor and collegiality at this crucial stage.  Best regards,  Sunita  Sunita Sen   PhD Scholar   Department of Computer Science   Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

full_email_context: Thread ID: X3HK7R Mail ID: MAIL7QBL1U2Z Date: 9th November 2024 From: JOCCH Editorial Office <editorial@jocch.acm.org> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in> CC: Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> Subject: Decision Notification: SUB-JOCCH-2024-0421 (Major Revision Required)  Dear Sunita Sen and co-authors,  We have now completed the peer review process for your manuscript, “Practical Workflows for NLP on International Historical Archival Data: Legal, Technical, and Community Lessons Learned,” submitted under Submission ID SUB-JOCCH-2024-0421. We thank you for your patience and for the meticulous effort evident in your work.  **Editorial Decision:** Major Revision  **Summary of Reviews:** The reviewers unanimously acknowledge the manuscript’s significant contributions, especially the rigor of your cross-jurisdictional legal compliance workflow and the depth provided in your supplementary “lessons learned” appendix. Several reviewers highlighted your comprehensive documentation of challenges intrinsic to multilingual, historical archival corpora and the transparency of your open-source NLP pipeline.  However, the feedback also calls for substantial revisions in the following domains: - **Methodological Clarity:** Reviewers request expanded details about corpus composition, preprocessing procedures, and annotation reliability, particularly for less-resourced language segments. - **Evaluation Metrics:** There is a need for a more granular breakdown of your benchmarking (by language/time period) and a discussion contextualizing F1 score variance in relation to OCR noise and archival source inconsistencies. - **Legal Framework Section:** While comprehensive, the section would be strengthened by a more explicit comparative table summarizing regional data-sharing constraints and actionable recommendations for practitioners. - **Supplementary Materials:** Minor formatting issues remain in the appendices and figure legends, and the editorial office requests all diagram sources be made available in editable format for future publication stages.  A consolidated PDF of detailed reviewer comments and the Associate Editor’s letter is attached via your author portal. We request that your revision submission include a point-by-point response letter addressing each review concern, as well as a tracked-changes manuscript.  **Timeline:** If you choose to pursue revision, please submit your revised files and response no later than 10th December 2022 to allow sufficient time for further review.  Should you have any queries or require clarification, please contact us referencing your Submission ID. We look forward to your resubmission and appreciate your continued interest in publishing with JOCCH.  Sincerely,  JOCCH Editorial Office   ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage   editorial@jocch.acm.org

full_email_context: Thread ID: WBAO7P Mail ID: MAILP8J4TCYV Date: 26th July 2023 From: Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> Subject: Presenter Checklist and Session Readiness (JCDL 2023 Rehearsal)  Dear Sunita, Ananya, and Michael,  Thank you, Sunita, for your careful coordination and for sending out the Zoom invitation and structured agenda for our rehearsal session later today. I am confident that this rehearsal will sharpen our delivery and refine our collaborative approach for the JCDL 2023 session.  As discussed, I am pleased to share the draft “Presenter Instructions” checklist with you ahead of our rehearsal. Attached to this email (and summarized below for quick reference) are the core guidelines tailored to JCDL’s latest handbook, and augmented by our collective insights:  1. **Speaker Introductions:** Each speaker should briefly state their research background, key project contributions, and their institution’s role. Please standardize to ~90 seconds each. 2. **Slide Management:** Ensure screen-sharing permissions are enabled prior to the session; designate Ananya as backup host for quick recovery if technical issues arise. 3. **Timekeeping Cues:** I will use a subtle hand gesture to indicate the 60-second warning for session transitions. Sunita, as session coordinator, may support this verbally if necessary. 4. **Q&A Moderation:** Michael to monitor audience questions (both chat and verbal), summarize queries, and call upon the intended responder. Ananya will serve as backup moderator. 5. **Contingency Preparedness:** In case of technical issues, the next listed speaker should immediately continue as per the run-order document. Keep backup PDFs and slide decks open locally. 6. **Session Recording & Ethics:** Remind the audience at the beginning about the session’s recording and privacy policies per JCDL guidelines. 7. **Key Takeaways:** Reiterate two to three main conclusions at the end, underscoring both methodological novelty and the societal relevance of NLP for historical data.  Please review and suggest any additions or revisions during today’s call. Michael, if you could also prepare your Q&A tip-sheet, that will be a valuable addendum to this checklist.  Looking forward to seeing everyone at 6:30 PM IST for our rehearsal. Thank you all for your enthusiasm and commitment—let’s make our JCDL 2023 session as impactful as our collaborative journey so far.  Best regards,  Ramesh  Prof. Ramesh Bhatia   Department of Computer Science   Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

full_email_context: Thread ID: PMG9HW Mail ID: MAILY56H2QMV Date: 18th April 2024 From: Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> Subject: Camera-ready Strategy and Action Points post-ACL Acceptance  Dear Sunita, Ramesh, and Ananya,  First, a heartfelt congratulations to the entire team for our acceptance at ACL 2024! It is gratifying to see the substantial work on harmonization and legal-operational flexibility in the historical NLP space being recognized at this level.   Having thoroughly examined the review reports and meta-review, I agree with the committee that the legal interoperability discussion and our multi-corpus pipeline stand out. To meet the camera-ready deadline of 13 March, I propose the following concrete steps:  1. **Minor Revisions**: Let’s address the reviewers’ notation regarding the expansion of “protocol-specific exceptions” in Section 4.3 and the clarity of annotation workflow in Figure 2. Sunita, perhaps you could lead on integrating these changes?  2. **Formatting Compliance**: Ananya, would you be able to do a technical pass, ensuring both metadata and PDF strictly adhere to the latest ACL camera-ready guidelines as soon as they’re circulated? There was also a comment about the graphical abstract for online proceedings—your visualization expertise would be invaluable here. 3. **Supplementary Materials**: Ramesh, could you ensure all supplementary datasets and code ZIPs referenced by DOI are fully accessible and that the data repository README files align with our updated manuscript terminology? 4. **Presenter Confirmation**: We need to confirm our designated presenter(s) by 13 March. Sunita, can you clarify your availability for an oral session, given your initial indication of interest?  Let’s aim to finalize all textual and technical updates by 9 March, which gives us a safety margin before the hard deadline. I’ve shared a new Overleaf branch (see “ACL2024_CameraReady_27Feb”) and a Google Drive folder for graphical assets.  Please reply with your availability for a short organizational video call sometime this week (preferably 1 or 2 March) to align on divisions of labor. Looking forward to working with you all as we cross this last milestone!  Best regards,  Michael  Dr. Michael Bradley   Department of Computer Science   Stanford University

object_label: sentiment lexicon usage analysis
evidence_sentence: My preliminary analyses reveal substantial variance in sentiment lexicon usage across decades
full_email_context: Thread ID: YLQR56 Mail ID: ZR71X3HB Date: 10th April 2019 From: Dr. Michael Bradley (michael@cs.stanford.edu) To: Sunita Sen (scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in), Prof. Ramesh Bhatia (ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in), Dr. Ananya Chatterjee (ananya.chatterjee@ox.ac.uk) Subject: Follow-up on Action Items and Experiment Design  Dear Team,  Thank you, Sunita, for sharing the comprehensive meeting minutes from our last discussion. I wanted to provide an update on my initial work and propose some strategies as we move into the experimental phase.  I have downloaded a representative subset from both the “Chronicling America” and “British Library Digital Collections” datasets, focusing on materials between 1880 and 1950, as this era features significant linguistic and socio-political shifts. My preliminary analyses reveal substantial variance in sentiment lexicon usage across decades, underscoring the need for robust temporal embeddings and alignment methods.  For our experiments, I suggest we implement a chronological split (by decade) rather than a random split, to better evaluate the temporal consistency of our models. Additionally, I propose we establish a baseline with LSTM and traditional lexicon-based approaches, before benchmarking Transformer models like BERT and its diachronic variants.  Ananya, your insight on interpretability will be vital—perhaps we can discuss model-agnostic methods such as LIME or SHAP? Sunita, please let us know if you encounter any challenges as you begin the data processing. Ramesh, could you recommend a schedule for our first progress check-in?  Looking forward to everyone's feedback.  Best regards, Michael

I have downloaded a representative subset from both the “Chronicling America” and “British Library Digital Collections” datasets, focusing on materials between 1880 and 1950, as this era features significant linguistic and socio-political shifts. My preliminary analyses reveal substantial variance in sentiment lexicon usage across decades, underscoring the need for robust temporal embeddings and alignment methods.  For our experiments, I suggest we implement a chronological split (by decade) rather than a random split, to better evaluate the temporal consistency of our models. Additionally, I propose we establish a baseline with LSTM and traditional lexicon-based approaches, before benchmarking Transformer models like BERT and its diachronic variants.  Ananya, your insight on interpretability will be vital—perhaps we can discuss model-agnostic methods such as LIME or SHAP? Sunita, please let us know if you encounter any challenges as you begin the data processing. Ramesh, could you recommend a schedule for our first progress check-in?  Looking forward to everyone's feedback.  Best regards, Michael

full_email_context: Thread ID: YLQR56 Mail ID: ZR71X3HB Date: 10th April 2019 From: Dr. Michael Bradley (michael@cs.stanford.edu) To: Sunita Sen (scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in), Prof. Ramesh Bhatia (ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in), Dr. Ananya Chatterjee (ananya.chatterjee@ox.ac.uk) Subject: Follow-up on Action Items and Experiment Design  Dear Team,  Thank you, Sunita, for sharing the comprehensive meeting minutes from our last discussion. I wanted to provide an update on my initial work and propose some strategies as we move into the experimental phase.  I have downloaded a representative subset from both the “Chronicling America” and “British Library Digital Collections” datasets, focusing on materials between 1880 and 1950, as this era features significant linguistic and socio-political shifts. My preliminary analyses reveal substantial variance in sentiment lexicon usage across decades, underscoring the need for robust temporal embeddings and alignment methods.  For our experiments, I suggest we implement a chronological split (by decade) rather than a random split, to better evaluate the temporal consistency of our models. Additionally, I propose we establish a baseline with LSTM and traditional lexicon-based approaches, before benchmarking Transformer models like BERT and its diachronic variants.  Ananya, your insight on interpretability will be vital—perhaps we can discuss model-agnostic methods such as LIME or SHAP? Sunita, please let us know if you encounter any challenges as you begin the data processing. Ramesh, could you recommend a schedule for our first progress check-in?  Looking forward to everyone's feedback.  Best regards, Michael

Michael, if you encountered additional notable segments while reviewing Dr. Patel’s comments, please share your recommendations as well.  Please let us know if you need further input after reviewing the updated metadata. Looking forward to seeing your draft figures as we continue refining the evaluation narrative.  Best regards, Sunita

All updated files can be found in the shared “JCDL2020_Presentation_Materials” folder.  If there are additional points you wish to add to the agenda, or if there are specific rehearsal tasks needed, please reply by tomorrow morning so we can maximize our 60-minute session. evidence_sentence: Thank you for the detailed update and for outlining the challenges in processing the historical datasets.
full_email_context: Thread ID: HZ5K7N Mail ID: DS4L8R2V Date: 16th April 2019 From: Dr. Michael Bradley (michael@cs.stanford.edu) To: Sunita Sen (scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in), Prof. Ramesh Bhatia (ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in), Dr. Ananya Chatterjee (ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk) Subject: Re: Data Processing Update and Preliminary Challenges  Dear Sunita and team,  Thank you for the detailed update and for outlining the challenges in processing the historical datasets. Your meticulous approach to standardizing metadata and addressing basic preprocessing steps is commendable, especially given the complexity of dealing with heterogeneous archival sources.  Regarding the OCR errors, from my experience in prior historical NLP projects, tools like Tesseract in combination with post-correction frameworks such as ‘ocropy’ or the recent deep learning–based approaches (e.g., Project LaVa) have shown decent improvement in text recovery. If computational resources allow, training a custom OCR correction model with a small manually verified subset can greatly boost accuracy for domain-specific errors typical of 19th-century newsprint. I can share a preprocessing workflow I used for digitized Stanford Library pamphlets if you wish.  For the metadata harmonization, I suggest we first analyze the prevalence of each date format and then standardized to the format most common or suitable for downstream chronological analysis. Where metadata is missing, probabilistic inference based on content or publication context might help, but as always, every imputation step should be well logged. A dual mapping system for each archive may also be pragmatic, provided we document all transformation rules for reproducibility.  Ananya, if you’re open to reviewing a targeted sample of the OCR-challenged segments, perhaps you and I can coordinate—to both improve cleaning and tie in interpretability insights for downstream models.  Looking forward to resolving these bottlenecks and making steady progress. Happy to do a brief demonstration of my correction workflow during our upcoming meeting, if that would be helpful.  Best regards, Michael

evidence_sentence: the distributed responsibilities for typesetting, licensing, figure integrity, and affiliation reporting—made the process smooth and error-free.
full_email_context: Thread ID: CZHAML Mail ID: MAILEZL7P8QX Date: 30th September 2023 From: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in> To: Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> Subject: Reflection on Proofing Process & Proposal for Documentation Practice  Dear all,  I hope this message finds you well. With the confirmation from the JOCCH editorial office regarding the completion of our proof corrections and the clear outline for the final publication stage, I wanted to echo Ramesh’s earlier suggestion and propose a more formalized approach to documenting our collaborative workflow.  Our coordinated handling of both the scientific and production aspects—especially the distributed responsibilities for typesetting, licensing, figure integrity, and affiliation reporting—made the process smooth and error-free. I strongly believe that capturing this experience in a living document will serve us well in upcoming projects, particularly as our cross-institutional team grows and new members join.   Would everyone be open to setting up a “Project Retrospective & Workflow Reference” folder in our existing Drive workspace? My idea is to summarize major communication points, reviewer allocation, proofing strategies, and rapid-response protocols for production queries. If agreeable, I’m happy to take the lead on compiling our process notes, with sections for each contributor’s perspective. This would help us benchmark effective practices and flag any areas that can be streamlined for next time.  Additionally, since JOCCH provided such a transparent production timeline, we could include a generic timeline template and example checklists for future submissions—whether for journals or conference proceedings like ACL and EMNLP.  Please let me know your thoughts on this proposal or if you have additional elements to recommend for documentation. If amenable, I can circulate a draft outline by next week for collective input.  Thank you again for the superb collaboration; I am proud to be part of this team and keen to carry forward our momentum.  Best regards,  Sunita  Sunita Sen   PhD Scholar, Department of Computer Science   Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

evidence_sentence: I have reviewed the request regarding further clarification of the annotation guidelines for entity disambiguation (Section 4.2)
full_email_context: Thread ID: BRYGQO Mail ID: MAILT7HXQW3L Date: 3rd December 2019 From: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in> To: Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> CC: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> Subject: Draft Illustrative Examples for Annotation Guidelines Update (JOCCH Minor Revisions)  Dear Ramesh, Ananya, and Michael,  Thank you, Ramesh, for the summary and clear distribution of action items in response to the editorial office’s decision. I have reviewed the request regarding further clarification of the annotation guidelines for entity disambiguation (Section 4.2), and have begun drafting concise illustrative examples based on our “Bengali-English Colonial Gazetteers” corpus. The goal is to highlight typical ambiguity cases, such as between administrative region names (e.g., “Murshidabad”) and personal or titular references (e.g., “Nawab of Murshidabad”), as well as entities reflected in both English and Bengali transliterations.  For the revision, I suggest including two brief, context-driven examples—one illustrating the annotation of a phrase where a region and a historical figure’s title overlap, and a second demonstrating a typical boundary case (such as a location wrongly recognized due to period-specific terminology). I am extracting these from our annotated set (“EntityAmbiguity_Examples_SSen_14Jan2020.docx”) for seamless integration into Section 4.2. I will also ensure both examples are aligned with the entity disambiguation protocol we established and cross-reference the supplementary guidelines.  I aim to circulate the draft text for review by 16 January. Please let me know if you have preferred cases from your review work that you believe would enhance these examples or if you wish to discuss the phrasing before integration. Ananya, do let me know if cross-verification with your Oxford team is feasible this week, particularly for historical context validation.   Thank you for your guidance and continued coordination as we move toward finalizing our manuscript.  Best wishes,  Sunita

full_email_context: Thread ID: BRYGQO Mail ID: MAILT7HXQW3L Date: 3rd December 2019 From: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in> To: Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> CC: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> Subject: Draft Illustrative Examples for Annotation Guidelines Update (JOCCH Minor Revisions)  Dear Ramesh, Ananya, and Michael,  Thank you, Ramesh, for the summary and clear distribution of action items in response to the editorial office’s decision. I have reviewed the request regarding further clarification of the annotation guidelines for entity disambiguation (Section 4.2), and have begun drafting concise illustrative examples based on our “Bengali-English Colonial Gazetteers” corpus. The goal is to highlight typical ambiguity cases, such as between administrative region names (e.g., “Murshidabad”) and personal or titular references (e.g., “Nawab of Murshidabad”), as well as entities reflected in both English and Bengali transliterations.  For the revision, I suggest including two brief, context-driven examples—one illustrating the annotation of a phrase where a region and a historical figure’s title overlap, and a second demonstrating a typical boundary case (such as a location wrongly recognized due to period-specific terminology). I am extracting these from our annotated set (“EntityAmbiguity_Examples_SSen_14Jan2020.docx”) for seamless integration into Section 4.2. I will also ensure both examples are aligned with the entity disambiguation protocol we established and cross-reference the supplementary guidelines.  I aim to circulate the draft text for review by 16 January. full_email_context: Thread ID: Y58D7K Mail ID: MAILE54MSZ19 Date: 19th March 2022 From: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in> To: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> Subject: General Audience Outreach Draft Uploaded & Next Steps  Dear Ananya, Michael, and Prof. Bhatia,  I am pleased to confirm that the general audience version of our outreach summary—intended for IACS news, university press offices, and social platforms—is now drafted and uploaded to our shared “JOCCH_Outreach_Drafts” folder. I based the tone on best practices for science communication to the public, focusing on accessibility, impact, and the significance of our interdisciplinary, international collaboration.  Key elements in this version: - An introductory paragraph contextualizing the importance of historical NLP for broad audiences. - Simplified explanations of our technical contributions and the regions/languages involved, avoiding specialist jargon where possible. - A dedicated segment on the dataset embargo, guided by Michael’s finalized statement, highlighting our commitment to responsible data stewardship. - Forward-looking remarks about public resource release after JOCCH publication and future educational workshops.  I invite your prompt feedback—Michael, your review of embargo and open-science language is especially valued. Ananya, thank you for leading the harmonization; I suggest we aim to synthesize both versions by 21 September so Prof. Bhatia can review for compliance and a unified institutional voice before external dissemination.  Additionally, please confirm if the 26 September internal call remains suitable for everyone, or if any adjustments are required.  Thank you all for your collaborative spirit and diligence. Looking forward to your suggestions and the final version of our outreach communications.  Best regards,  Sunita  Sunita Sen   PhD Scholar   Department of Computer Science   Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

object_label: Stanford University’s Office of Communications approval of JCDL 2022 press release
evidence_sentence: I am delighted to report that, as of this afternoon (Pacific Time), Stanford University’s Office of Communications has officially approved our JCDL 2022 press release.
full_email_context: Thread ID: HOLJGN Mail ID: MAILL7P3V2SB Date: 13th August 2022 From: Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> To: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> Subject: Stanford Press Office Approval – Final Synchronization  Dear Ananya, Sunita, and Ramesh,  I am delighted to report that, as of this afternoon (Pacific Time), Stanford University’s Office of Communications has officially approved our JCDL 2022 press release. Ms. Christine Wong sent formal clearance (attached: “Stanford_Approval_JCDL2022.pdf”) confirming that the document meets all institutional standards – including legal, attributional, and global partnership guidelines. Christine expressed her appreciation for our collaborative diligence and requested that we notify her as soon as the release timeline is set, to enable Stanford’s media relations team to coordinate targeted outreach and embargo lifting in tandem with IACS and Oxford.  Thank you all for your extraordinary teamwork in navigating this multi-office approval process so efficiently. Sunita, thank you for sharing IACS’s official approval and for centralizing all documentation in the shared folder – I have uploaded the Stanford clearance to /InstitutionalApprovals/Stanford for group access. Ramesh, your outlined protocol has served us well in maintaining seamless updates among the partners. Ananya, if Oxford’s public affairs team provides their final sign-off in the coming days, we should be poised to schedule both the internal “all-clear” email and the external announcement.  Next steps: - @Ananya: Please inform us as soon as Oxford’s clearance comes through, or if there are any comments to adjudicate. - @All: Pending Oxford’s sign-off, I recommend a brief Google Meet/Zoom (20 minutes) to harmonize any residual details and fix a synchronized release date, as discussed. - I will also prepare a draft “all-clear” notification for the JCDL 2022 communications liaison, so we can promptly finalize media distribution logistics across all institutions.  Thanks again for your exceptional collaboration. Looking forward to our imminent media launch!  Warm regards,  Michael  Dr. Michael Bradley   Department of Computer Science   Stanford University

full_email_context: Thread ID: N55V3R Mail ID: MAILA93SVWX7 Date: 4th August 2019 From: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in> To: Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> Subject: Re: Submission Decision Notification – Planning for Minor Revisions (SUB-JOCCH-2019-0187)  Dear Prof. Bhatia, Michael, and Ananya,  Thank you all for your exceptional teamwork throughout the review process, and for your attention to detail which has clearly contributed to the positive outcome in the JOCCH decision. I am delighted by the strongly supportive feedback from the reviewers and the formal “Minor Revision Required” decision—congratulations to all.  I have read through the editorial summary and the reviewer reports attached to the latest JOCCH notification (SUB-JOCCH-2019-0187). All three reviewers’ comments are constructive and quite focused. I propose the following plan based on the required changes: 1. **Expansion of the “Limitations and Future Work” Section:** I recommend drafting a new subsection specifically addressing domain shift issues in non-English OCR segments. Ananya, would you be willing to take the lead here, summarizing relevant observations from the technical appendix and your background analyses on corpus diversity? 2. **Illustrative Table on Annotator Agreement:** Michael, could you please extract and summarize the inter-annotator agreement metrics by genre (as noted in the reviewer report)? I can assist with formatting and integrating it into the results section. 3. **Compliance Appendix Clarifications:** Prof. Bhatia, it would be helpful if you could review the current compliance appendix and propose clarifications or additional language regarding archival licensing terms, reflecting the reviewer’s queries.  I will begin drafting a template for our point-by-point response letter, mapping each reviewer comment to the corresponding planned change. If agreeable, we could schedule a coordination meeting early next week (Monday or Tuesday IST) to discuss progress and agree on a concrete timeline, ensuring enough time for review and final edits before our 22 September deadline.  Please confirm your availability and let me know if you have alternative suggestions or concerns about these assignments. Thank you again, and I look forward to our swift and successful revision!  Best regards,  Sunita

I want to formally acknowledge receipt of the JCDL 2023 camera-ready submission acknowledgment (SUB-JCDL-2023-0427) and thank the committee for their timely communication.   As we await any follow-up requests from the proceedings chair, I suggest that we use this interim period to further refine our session delivery strategy. While the submitted materials are finalized, our live presentation can benefit greatly from a brief run-through, particularly with respect to time management and seamless transitions. Based on previous JCDL experiences, a succinct, well-coordinated opening statement and closing summary tend to leave a strong impression.   With this in mind, I propose the following next steps: 1. Schedule a brief coordination call next week to rehearse our live introductions and closing remarks, and to discuss approaches for engaging with audience questions. 2. Review any correspondence from the JCDL committee for last-minute updates or requirements. I will monitor our inboxes closely for alerts regarding formatting or technical adjustments. 3. Circulate a draft “Presenter Instructions” checklist (I will prepare this) based on previous years’ guidelines and this year’s preliminary conference handbook, to ensure we are fully prepared.  Please indicate your availability for a rehearsal call between 17–21 April, or suggest alternative slots if needed. If there are specific topics or audience engagement strategies anyone would like to discuss, feel free to highlight them in your reply.  Congratulations again on reaching this key milestone, and thank you all for your professionalism and collegiality. I look forward to continuing our collaboration as we prepare for our JCDL 2023 session.  Best regards,  Ramesh  Prof. Ramesh Bhatia   Department of Computer Science   Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

full_email_context: Thread ID: AT50K2 Mail ID: MAIL3PA7YZXT Date: 25th October 2020 From: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in> To: Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> Subject: Planning and Task Allocation for JOCCH Minor Revision (SUB-JOCCH-2020-0047)  Dear Ramesh, Michael, and Ananya,  Thank you all for your ongoing collaboration on our JOCCH manuscript. I have carefully reviewed the editorial decision email on SUB-JOCCH-2020-0047 and summarized the main revision requests outlined by the reviewers. To organize our efforts efficiently given the 18th November 2019 deadline, I propose the following breakdown of tasks and next steps:  1. **Domain Shift Analysis (Reviewer 1's comment):**    - I will prepare an expanded section on the transferability limits, focusing on the observed behaviors as the model is applied across Gujarati and French datasets. Michael, could you help review the statistical framing and ensure consistency with our earlier cross-validation setup? I expect to have a draft of the domain shift paragraphs and supporting plots by 5 February.  2. **Code Anchor System Methodology (Reviewer 2's request):**    - Ananya, since you coordinated the integration of the cell anchors, would you be able to draft a short methods subsection highlighting how the anchor system enhances transparency and reviewer navigation? I can contribute with a concrete figure if you think it’s helpful.  3. **Ethical Data Sourcing & Compliance (Reviewer 3's point):**    - Ramesh, would you be able to review and expand our text regarding local regulatory compliance and anonymization, particularly to address the new recommendation for explicit mention of regional data governance protocols?  4. **Editing and Table Integration:**    - I will revise Section 2.2 to ensure clarity and brevity as suggested, and draft a new summary table mapping error types to privacy-preservation strategies. I’ll circulate the first version via our Drive folder by 7 February for your collective input.  **Proposed Timeline:** - Initial drafts by 7 February - Internal feedback and integration: 10–14 February - Final revision ready for pre-submission checks by 22 February  Please confirm your availability for contributions in the suggested areas, or if you would prefer to adjust the allocations. I suggest we schedule a check-in call during the week of 8 February to review progress and resolve any overlapping issues—once you provide your availability, I’ll propose meeting times.  Looking forward to your feedback and to jointly delivering a clear and robust revision for JOCCH.  Best regards,  Sunita

I have carefully reviewed the editorial decision email on SUB-JOCCH-2020-0047 and summarized the main revision requests outlined by the reviewers. To organize our efforts efficiently given the 18th November 2019 deadline, I propose the following breakdown of tasks and next steps:  1. **Domain Shift Analysis (Reviewer 1's comment):**    - I will prepare an expanded section on the transferability limits, focusing on the observed behaviors as the model is applied across Gujarati and French datasets. Michael, could you help review the statistical framing and ensure consistency with our earlier cross-validation setup? I expect to have a draft of the domain shift paragraphs and supporting plots by 5 February.  2. **Code Anchor System Methodology (Reviewer 2's request):**    - Ananya, since you coordinated the integration of the cell anchors, would you be able to draft a short methods subsection highlighting how the anchor system enhances transparency and reviewer navigation? I can contribute with a concrete figure if you think it’s helpful.  3. **Ethical Data Sourcing & Compliance (Reviewer 3's point):**    - Ramesh, would you be able to review and expand our text regarding local regulatory compliance and anonymization, particularly to address the new recommendation for explicit mention of regional data governance protocols?  4. **Editing and Table Integration:**    - I will revise Section 2.2 to ensure clarity and brevity as suggested, and draft a new summary table mapping error types to privacy-preservation strategies. I’ll circulate the first version via our Drive folder by 7 February for your collective input.  **Proposed Timeline:** - Initial drafts by 7 February - Internal feedback and integration: 10–14 February - Final revision ready for pre-submission checks by 22 February  Please confirm your availability for contributions in the suggested areas, or if you would prefer to adjust the allocations. I suggest we schedule a check-in call during the week of 8 February to review progress and resolve any overlapping issues—once you provide your availability, I’ll propose meeting times.  Looking forward to your feedback and to jointly delivering a clear and robust revision for JOCCH.  Best regards,  Sunita

I have reviewed the revised figures and supplementary files in our GitHub repository and confirm that, from my end, file names, in-text linkage, and all main-to-supplement references follow the proposed JOCCH standards. Michael, your suggestion to use the “Supplementary Figure/Table Sx” system is very clear—I look forward to your draft template for standardized captions, which I believe will be highly beneficial as we finalize the manuscript.  Ananya, I have also cross-checked your Hindi/Urdu vignettes alongside my Bengali/English contributions. All narrative and guideline references appear harmonized and explicit, satisfying both internal and external reproducibility expectations. Having integrated everyone’s feedback, I believe our case study corpus is both comprehensive and well-structured for review.  Prof. Bhatia—thank you for confirming initial ethics compliance; please keep us informed should any conditions arise from IACS’s legal review so we can adjust hosting permissions or protocols swiftly.  **Action Items (from my side):** - Will review Michael’s forthcoming caption template upon receipt and apply consistently across all supplementary references before the full manuscript’s circulation on 24 August. - Am available for a call or email exchange if any last-minute terminology or linking issues are detected—preferably by 23 August to allow adequate buffer pre-submission.  Thank you all for your expertise and collaborative spirit in bringing this multi-institutional project so close to submission-readiness. Looking forward to your feedback and the finalization phase.  Best wishes,  Sunita  Sunita Sen   PhD Scholar   Department of Computer Science   Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

Ananya, your offer to help with the slide deck is much appreciated—feel free to reach out if you would like further inputs on the Bengali-English corpus normalization section.  Looking forward to everyone’s final confirmation and to a productive discussion on 7th April.  Best wishes,  Sunita

full_email_context: Thread ID: A9CPIQ Mail ID: MAIL1DXV7GFS Date: 31st October 2020 From: Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> Subject: Compliance and Anonymization Update – Ready for Review  Dear Sunita, Ananya, and Michael,  Thank you all for your substantial efforts over the past week. I am pleased to confirm that my draft for the revised ethical data sourcing and anonymization sections is now complete and available for your review in the shared Drive (“Compliance_Anonymization_v1_Feb2021.docx”). In light of Reviewer 3’s comments, I have:   - Provided explicit references to compliance protocols governing both the Indian (IT Act, 2019 and the 2019 guidelines) and European (GDPR Article 89, Recital 156) datasets included in our study. - Detailed our anonymization pipeline, including data hashing procedures, exclusion of personally identifiable information at the source, and our approach to managing regional digital archival consent. - Added a compliance justification table that itemizes each requirement raised by the reviewers, cross-referenced to manuscript subsections and institutional approval documentation. - Cited recent best-practice case studies (including those from the Journal of Documentation and ACM JOCCH) where similar protocols were endorsed.  Sunita, I have referenced the error-type privacy table you are preparing under Section 2.2, and suggested how its integration can further highlight our privacy-preservation strategies.  Michael and Ananya, I welcome your feedback both on technical completeness and the clarity of regulatory references. Ananya, I have aligned my narrative to the anchor methods subsection, explicitly inviting reviewers to verify compliance claims via the annotated code anchors.  Please provide your comments or direct edits by 9 February so that I can address any outstanding items before our group call. I am confident that this comprehensive update, paired with our other revisions, positions us to meet the 1 March submission deadline and satisfy all reviewer concerns.  Thank you all for your diligent collaboration, and I look forward to our continued progress.  Best regards,  Ramesh

Thank you all for your diligent collaboration, and I look forward to our continued progress.  Best regards,  Ramesh

full_email_context: Thread ID: JZPXSE Mail ID: MAILRM2TCL89 Date: 14th September 2022 From: Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> To: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu>, Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in> Subject: Re: JCDL 2022—Follow-Up: Technical Requirements & Conference Liaison Update  Dear Ananya, Michael, and Sunita,  Thank you, Ananya, for your efficient communication with the JCDL organizing team and for compiling such a clear list of action points in your last email. The confirmation regarding Zoom, the format requirements, and especially the recommendation for an accessibility-compliant, pre-recorded backup video are all extremely helpful as we finalize our preparations.  I will take responsibility for auditing our current slide deck for accessibility. In particular, I will ensure that alt-text is provided for every image, chart, and diagram and review the colour contrast and font choices for screen-reader compatibility. Ananya, your offer of assistance is much appreciated—if you notice any persistent gaps or best practice examples from Oxford’s experience, please do share them, as we want to make the deck exemplary. I intend to complete this review by 20 April and will upload the revised slides to the shared drive.  Sunita, once your draft of the pre-recorded presentation is available, feel free to share a preliminary version even before it is fully polished. This will allow us all to comment and incorporate refinements at an early stage, especially around pacing and clarity for possible international audiences.  Michael, thank you in advance for adding the finalized session summary and the compiled biographies to our asset folder; a brief email notification once uploaded will help maintain our documentation audit trail for any future reference.  Let us continue this well-coordinated momentum. If anyone anticipates being away or needing to adjust their timeline for these deliverables, please communicate early. It’s a privilege working with such a meticulous and reliable team.  Best regards,  Ramesh  Prof. Ramesh Bhatia   Department of Computer Science   Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

full_email_context: Thread ID: I990OC Mail ID: MAILR4TB9SCM Date: 19th July 2023 From: Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> To: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> Subject: Final Materials Review and Camera-Ready Submission Checklist (JCDL 2023)  Dear Sunita, Ramesh, and Ananya,  Many thanks, Sunita, for the thorough debrief note and for prompt circulation of next steps post-rehearsal. I have carefully reviewed the run-order document as well as the latest Q&A edits—both are superbly organized and strike just the right balance between technical depth and clarity for the expected JCDL audience.  As promised, I’ve incorporated clarifications regarding the pipeline’s multilingual generalizability and added a short slide about parallel annotation results on the lesser-represented language samples. These are now uploaded to the shared folder (“Final Deck v3.4” and “Q&A_JCDL2023_FINAL.docx”). Ananya, your previous suggestions on axis labeling and handover cues have been implemented, with alternate phrasing options provided for review.  Before we proceed to upload the camera-ready materials and supplementary documents to the JCDL system, I suggest we each take a final pass through the shared Google Drive archive to check for version mismatches or minor formatting glitches (especially on embedded media or hyperlinks). Ramesh, could you please reconfirm the details on affiliations and funding acknowledgments? Sunita, if you can ensure the updated run-order and backup PDF are duly labeled as “camera_ready” versions, that would avoid last-minute confusion.  Assuming no critical edits arise, I propose we initiate submission by 13 April, thereby building in an extra day margin before the formal deadline. Please confirm your go-ahead or flag any last concerns by end of day today (12 April), Stanford time, so that we can coordinate a smooth and timely submission as a team.  Looking forward to crossing this important milestone together.  Best regards,  Michael  Dr. Michael Bradley   Department of Computer Science   Stanford University

full_email_context: Thread ID: UOT38J Mail ID: MAIL9DS4K1QM Date: 13th October 2024 From: Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> To: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> Subject: RE: Acknowledgment of Integrated Draft & Review Plan  Dear Ananya, Sunita, and Ramesh,  Thank you all for your swift responses and the coordinated approach to these final review stages. Sunita, your collation and layering of the disparate section materials into a cohesive draft is exemplary, and Ananya, your commitment to a thorough tracked-changes review is much appreciated.  A few immediate updates from my side ahead of the 24 September internal feedback deadline:  1. **“Lessons Learned” Summary:** I have started drafting both a succinct summary for the technical note appendix and an expanded outline for a potential blog post, as proposed by Ananya. Initial reflections cluster around the following: (a) pragmatics of cross-institutional legal harmonization, (b) the necessity of modular compliance workflows (as seen with the Zenodo pipeline), and (c) embedded documentation for reproducibility in historical NLP. I will circulate these documents in our shared folder for your review and suggestions by early tomorrow.  2. **Figures and Diagrams:** I have double-checked the latest placements and legends for our workflow and “pitfall node” diagrams in the current draft. I echo the suggestion to use Sunita’s comparative matrix as the basis for our decision at the next meeting.  I am available for a brief sync or follow-up clarification at your convenience between now and the official review deadline. As a group, we should aim for a consolidated set of final edits and a venue decision by no later than 25 September, in order to keep our submission process smooth and timely.  Thank you for your diligence and collegiality as we approach the finish line. I look forward to integrating Ananya’s review and finalizing our submission plan.  Best regards,  Michael  Dr. Michael Bradley   Department of Computer Science   Stanford University

full_email_context: Thread ID: VROL1L Mail ID: MAILE7ZRH6U9 Date: 1st June 2020 From: Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> To: Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu>, Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> Subject: Re: Additional Agenda Item – Data Licensing & Repository Sustainability  Dear Michael, Sunita, and Ananya,  Thank you, Michael, for highlighting the importance of data licensing and repository sustainability in advance of our meeting. I strongly agree that addressing these aspects now will ease the submission and review process for JOCCH, and help ensure our research output remains accessible to the wider community.  From the IACS perspective, there are a few institutional requirements to keep in mind: 1. For datasets deriving from national archives or government records, we must reference the specific source archive’s reuse policy, which sometimes limits redistribution outside academia unless explicit permissions are granted. 2. IACS generally recommends the adoption of CC BY or CC BY-NC licenses. I propose defaulting to CC BY for the bulk of our repository, with CC BY-NC applied selectively for sensitive/embargoed components. We must clearly document any ancillary access restrictions within the main README and submission supplement. 3. To ensure long-term sustainability, IACS supports depositing final versions of all datasets and code to both a global repository (such as Zenodo) and to our institutional archive, with clear instructions for periodic review. Assigning a maintenance contact, as you suggested, is advisable.  Ananya and Sunita, do Oxford or IACS have additional requirements regarding dual-institutional hosting or compliance for multi-institutional projects? We should at minimum ensure license compatibility and alignment on proprietary data handling.  I propose allocating the final 10 minutes of our meeting to collectively draft a compliance and licensing statement that reflects the above points. Michael, thank you again for preparing the compliance summary—please flag any points requiring urgent attention before we circulate the repository more widely.  Looking forward to our discussion, and wishing everyone a productive weekend in the meantime.  Best regards,  Ramesh

full_email_context: Thread ID: VROL1L Mail ID: MAILE7ZRH6U9 Date: 1st June 2020 From: Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in> To: Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu>, Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> Subject: Re: Additional Agenda Item – Data Licensing & Repository Sustainability  Dear Michael, Sunita, and Ananya,  Thank you, Michael, for highlighting the importance of data licensing and repository sustainability in advance of our meeting. I strongly agree that addressing these aspects now will ease the submission and review process for JOCCH, and help ensure our research output remains accessible to the wider community.  From the IACS perspective, there are a few institutional requirements to keep in mind: 1. For datasets deriving from national archives or government records, we must reference the specific source archive’s reuse policy, which sometimes limits redistribution outside academia unless explicit permissions are granted. 2. IACS generally recommends the adoption of CC BY or CC BY-NC licenses. I propose defaulting to CC BY for the bulk of our repository, with CC BY-NC applied selectively for sensitive/embargoed components. We must clearly document any ancillary access restrictions within the main README and submission supplement. 3. To ensure long-term sustainability, IACS supports depositing final versions of all datasets and code to both a global repository (such as Zenodo) and to our institutional archive, with clear instructions for periodic review. Assigning a maintenance contact, as you suggested, is advisable.  Ananya and Sunita, do Oxford or IACS have additional requirements regarding dual-institutional hosting or compliance for multi-institutional projects? We should at minimum ensure license compatibility and alignment on proprietary data handling.  I propose allocating the final 10 minutes of our meeting to collectively draft a compliance and licensing statement that reflects the above points. Michael, thank you again for preparing the compliance summary—please flag any points requiring urgent attention before we circulate the repository more widely.  Looking forward to our discussion, and wishing everyone a productive weekend in the meantime.  Best regards,  Ramesh

full_email_context: Thread ID: MFZS4B Mail ID: MAILVR69CHU8 Date: 8th November 2021 From: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk> To: Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> Subject: Re: Proposed Time Slots for Dry Run – ACL 2021 Oral Presentation  Dear Prof. Bhatia, Sunita, and Michael,  Thank you for circulating the proposed time slots for our upcoming dry run and for the ongoing collaborative energy as we finalize preparations for the ACL 2021 oral session. I am pleased to confirm my availability for both the 24 April (5:30–7:00 pm IST) and 25 April (6:00–7:30 pm IST) slots, with a preference for 24 April if that proves convenient for the majority. The provided Zoom link works seamlessly for me.  Sunita, I look forward to reviewing your draft slides and echo Michael’s suggestion for a clear visual comparison between the traditional and provenance-aware metrics. If you could include one or two annotated historical samples illustrating how our annotation protocol adapts across datasets, that would further strengthen our narrative for a diverse audience. Please share the PowerPoint file at your earliest convenience so I can provide detailed feedback ahead of our meeting.  During the dry run, I propose we allocate a few minutes at the end to discuss how to succinctly address expected questions regarding generalizability of our synthetic instance protocol, since I anticipate this may arise during the Q&A session at ACL. I am happy to synthesize a few key talking points on this and share them before the rehearsal.  Thank you again for this coordinated effort—looking forward to an engaging practice session and a compelling conference presentation with you all.  Best regards,  Ananya   Dr. Ananya Chatterjee   Department of Computer Science   University of Oxford

full_email_context: Thread ID: 886TQR Mail ID: MAIL62VJZD1M Date: 20th June 2024 From: Sunita Sen <scholar.sunita@iacs.res.in> To: Dr. Ananya Chatterjee <ananya.chatterjee@cs.ox.ac.uk>, Prof. Ramesh Bhatia <ramesh.bhatia@iacs.res.in>, Dr. Michael Bradley <michael@cs.stanford.edu> Subject: Confirmation of Attendance & Agenda Suggestions for 11 May Coordination Call  Dear Ananya, Ramesh, and Michael,  Thank you, Ananya, for taking the initiative to organize the final coordination call and for circulating the Zoom details and a clear agenda. I am pleased to confirm my attendance for the meeting today, 16:00–17:00 IST. The time works well for me, and I look forward to wrapping up any residual queries before our internal draft deadline.  I have reviewed the proposed agenda and would like to suggest adding a brief discussion point regarding the candidate cover letter for the JOCCH submission. In particular, I believe it may be strategic to highlight our collaborative legal practices and the structured meta-annotation process in the cover letter, as these have been recurring recommendations in recent issues of the journal. If there is time, perhaps we can designate one of us (I am happy to draft an initial version) to circulate a template following the meeting.  Additionally, I have double-checked the final Zenodo preview link Michael posted—everything appears consistent with our manuscript, and no inconsistencies or typos stood out to me. I will bring a couple of minor clarification questions regarding the embargo status of a dataset subset, but these are easily resolved during the call.  Thank you all for your diligence and thoughtful teamwork as we approach this submission milestone. Looking forward to a productive discussion later today.  Best regards,  Sunita  Sunita Sen   PhD Scholar   Department of Computer Science   Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science

I propose defaulting to CC BY for the bulk of our repository, with CC BY-NC applied selectively for sensitive/embargoed components. We must clearly document any ancillary access restrictions within the main README and submission supplement. 3. Assigning a maintenance contact, as you suggested, is advisable.  Ananya and Sunita, do Oxford or IACS have additional requirements regarding dual-institutional hosting or compliance for multi-institutional projects?
